emergency.heading: Malta emergency number:
emergency.detail: Dial 112 for the police, an ambulance or the fire service anywhere in Malta, Gozo and Comino. The Malta Police Force says the call is free from any phone, even one without a SIM card. If you have a hearing or speech impairment, the police textphone service is 7977 0112.
notices: Dial 112 anywhere in Malta, Gozo or Comino for the police, an ambulance or the fire service. The call is free from any phone.
Mater Dei Hospital in Msida runs the main Accident & Emergency department, listed on +356 2545 4030. On Gozo, Gozo General Hospital in Victoria is on +356 2344 6000.

faqs.question: What is the emergency number in Malta?
faqs.answer: Dial 112. It reaches the police, an ambulance and the fire service across Malta, Gozo and Comino. The Malta Police Force says calls to 112 are free and can be made from any phone, even without a SIM card. If you have a hearing or speech impairment, the police textphone service is 7977 0112.

faqs.question: Can I call the emergency services in English?
faqs.answer: The Malta Police Force says it provides information in Maltese and English. English is one of Malta's two official languages, alongside Maltese, and the Malta Tourism Authority says English is understood wherever you go. Give your location first (town, street, a landmark or the name of the beach), then say what has happened.

faqs.question: Which hospital do I go to in an emergency in Malta or Gozo?
faqs.answer: Call 112 for an ambulance, or go straight to Accident & Emergency. On the main island this is Mater Dei Hospital in Msida (A&E +356 2545 4030, switchboard +356 2545 0000). On Gozo it is Gozo General Hospital in Victoria (+356 2344 6000), which says it is linked to Mater Dei by 24/7 air and land ambulance services for emergency and specialised care. Mater Dei also lists a Medicines and Poisons Info Office on +356 2545 6508.

faqs.question: Who do I call for an emergency at sea, on a boat or while diving?
faqs.answer: Dial 112. The Armed Forces of Malta say their Operations Centre is the national Search and Rescue Coordination Centre, and that a call to 112 is routed straight to it when AFM help is needed. Mater Dei Hospital lists a Hyperbaric Unit (+356 2545 5269) for diving injuries, but in an emergency call 112 first. The UK Foreign Office notes that people drown in Malta every year: swim where lifeguards and flags are, and treat a red flag as a warning to stay out.

faqs.question: How do I report a theft or another crime in Malta?
faqs.answer: If anyone is in danger or the crime is happening now, dial 112. For an incident that is already over, report it at a police station or use the Malta Police remote report service: you book a callback online, an officer takes the report by phone or video call, and you receive a police report number for your insurer. Police General Headquarters in Floriana is on +356 2122 4001. The UK Foreign Office warns of pickpocketing on crowded buses between Valletta and St Julian's and of drink spiking in some Paceville bars.

faqs.question: I lost my passport in Malta: who do I contact?
faqs.answer: Report the loss to the police, then contact your own country's mission. The British High Commission is at Whitehall Mansions, Ta' Xbiex Seafront; GOV.UK lists its general consular number as +356 2323 0000. Its online contact page also provides a route to call 24/7 in an emergency. Family in the UK can call the Foreign Office in London on +44 20 7008 5000 (24 hours). The US Embassy is at Ta' Qali National Park, Attard, on +356 2561 4000, the number it gives for US citizens with emergencies, including outside office hours.

faqs.question: Does my EHIC or GHIC work in Malta?
faqs.answer: Yes, for medically necessary state healthcare. The European Commission says treatment in public hospitals and health centres is free with a valid EHIC, and that medicines prescribed as an in-patient and for three days after discharge are free, while later prescriptions are paid in full. The UK Foreign Office says UK visitors need a GHIC or EHIC for state care, and the NHS says a GHIC is not a replacement for travel insurance: it does not cover private clinics or repatriation. Visitors insured only in the USA should arrange travel insurance; EHIC eligibility depends on public health insurance coverage, not nationality.

faqs.question: Where can I find a pharmacy open on a Sunday or public holiday?
faqs.answer: Pharmacies in Malta and Gozo open on Sundays, public holidays and Saturdays on a roster published by the Malta Medicines Authority on its Pharmacy Roster page. The UK Foreign Office says UK prescriptions are not recognised in Malta and that you can ask to see a private GP at most pharmacies.

essentials.advisory: The U.S. State Department lists Malta at Level 1: Exercise normal precautions, its lowest level, in an advisory issued on 9 July 2026 and unchanged when we checked in November 2026. It calls Malta generally safe and warns that riptides have caused drowning deaths among tourists. The UK Foreign Office, whose Malta page was last updated on 11 August 2026, says crime against tourists is rare but reports pickpocketing on buses between Valletta and St Julian's and drink spiking in some Paceville bars. A GHIC or EHIC gives access to medically necessary state healthcare, but the Foreign Office says it is not an alternative to travel insurance.

tips.label: Tap water
tips.text: Tap water is treated to EU standards: the Water Services Corporation says Malta's tap water exceeds the strictest European standards for safety and taste, and explains that it adds small amounts of chlorine to keep the supply safe to drink, which some people can taste. Follow any notice from your accommodation

tips.label: Sun
tips.text: Use sunscreen and stay hydrated: cover up, drink water through the day and keep out of the midday sun in summer, especially on beaches and coastal walks

tips.label: Mosquitoes
tips.text: Mosquito repellent: worth packing for warm evenings outdoors

tips.label: At the beach
tips.text: The UK Foreign Office says lifeguards patrol most beaches in summer and use a flag system, with red flags marking dangerous conditions, and that some beaches have strong undercurrents. The U.S. State Department warns that riptides have caused drowning deaths among tourists. Swim within marked zones, take extra care where there are no lifeguards or flags, and do not dive into water of unknown depth.

tips.label: On the road
tips.text: Malta drives on the left. The UK Foreign Office says some roads are in poor condition and local driving standards are poor, and the U.S. State Department describes roads as narrow and congested. On buses, keep your valuables in sight: the Foreign Office reports pickpocketing on crowded routes between Valletta and St Julian's in summer.

guides.title: Best Beaches in Malta, Gozo and Comino: An Honest Guide
guides.summary: The best beaches in Malta grouped by who they suit, from Mellieha Bay and Golden Bay to Ramla, San Blas and the Blue Lagoon, with honest notes on crowds, access and sea conditions.
guides.html:
How to choose a beach in Malta

Malta is not a long-sandy-beach destination in the way the Algarve or Crete are. The islands are mostly limestone, so a lot of swimming happens off flat rock, from ladders and from small coves. The sandy beaches that do exist are concentrated in the north-west and north of Malta, on Gozo's north coast, and in a few man-made or replenished bays in town. Knowing which type you want saves a wasted bus ride.

This guide groups 20 beaches by what they suit: sandy family beaches, quieter bays that take a walk, rock swimming, Gozo, and Comino. Each name links to its own page with directions. For the swimming season, see our best time to visit Malta; VisitMalta notes that beach life lasts well into October.

Flags, lifeguards and Blue Flag status

The Malta Tourism Authority (MTA) manages nine beaches directly and supports eight more, including some on Gozo and Comino. On managed beaches, a red-over-yellow flag marks the lifeguarded zone. Green means calm water, yellow a medium hazard and red a high hazard, while a double red flag means the water is closed. A purple flag means pests such as stinging jellyfish are present: if you see one, stay out and ask the lifeguard for advice.

The Blue Flag is an annual award for water quality, safety, services and environmental management, run in Malta by Nature Trust FEE Malta. The list changes every season. As of November 2026, Blue Flag Malta's undated online directory lists Mellieha Bay, Golden Bay, Ghajn Tuffieha Bay, Bugibba Perched Beach, Qawra Point, Fond Ghadir, St George's Bay and the Med-Bar Reef Club (Westin Dragonara), plus Marsalforn Bay, Hondoq ir-Rummien and Ramla l-Hamra Bay on Gozo. The directory does not identify an award year, so confirm the award for your travel season. One fixed point: the MTA says Malta's first Blue Flag went to St George's Bay in 2009. Our emergency contacts page has the numbers to keep on your phone.

Sandy beaches for families

Mellieha Bay (Għadira)

Mellieha Bay, also called Ghadira, is the largest of thirteen pocket beaches around Mellieha and an obvious choice with children. VisitMalta describes its low-gradient sand and clear, shallow water as making it the most popular family beach on the island. It has restaurants, water sports zones and wheelchair access, and the Ghadira Nature Reserve wetland sits just behind it. Expect it to be full on summer weekends. It is a short ride from Mellieha village.

Golden Bay

Golden Bay is one of the most popular north-west beaches: wide sand facing west, with facilities in season. It suits families who want everything in one place, and it is one of Malta's most popular sandy beaches. Arrive early in July and August.

Ghajn Tuffieha Bay (Riviera)

Next door, Ghajn Tuffieha (Għajn Tuffieħa) is the more scenic of the pair, an undeveloped bay below a clay hillside managed as a protected area. The catch is access: VisitMalta says the beach can only be reached down a steep flight of steps or by a gravel track, which is hard work with a pushchair. It is usually less crowded than Golden Bay. The official listing also warns that it is prone to strong currents when the wind is from the north-west, and the MTA defines a red flag as high hazard. Ask the lifeguard before entering.

Bugibba Perched Beach

The Bugibba Perched Beach is a man-made stretch of sand, about 2,000 square metres, laid on the rocky shore of the promenade in St Paul's Bay. Platforms lead into the sea, one of them wheelchair accessible. It is small, but useful if you are staying in Bugibba or Qawra and want sand without a bus ride.

St George's Bay, St Julian's

St George's Bay is a small sandy beach in the middle of the hotel and nightlife district of St Julian's. It is convenient rather than scenic and gets very crowded in summer, but you can walk there from most hotels in the area.

Pretty Bay, Birzebbuga

Pretty Bay in Birzebbuga (Birżebbuġa) in the south-east was artificially filled with sand recovered during nearby dredging works, and is now one of Malta's larger sandy beaches. It sits right in town with shops and restaurants along the front. Come for convenience rather than scenery.

Armier Bay

Armier Bay at the northern tip faces Comino and Gozo, with beach bars but no hotels. It is popular with Maltese families at weekends. VisitMalta notes it can get rough swells because it is exposed to north winds, so check the flags on breezy days.

Quieter bays that need a walk

Gnejna Bay

Gnejna Bay (Ġnejna), near the village of Mgarr, is usually less crowded than its neighbours. There is a sandy beach, flat rocks for sunbathing on one side and a rougher walk along the shore to quieter spots. Some facilities open in season.

Paradise Bay

Paradise Bay is a sandy cove at the very north of Malta, close to the Cirkewwa ferry terminal, with clear water and a view of Comino. It is small, so it fills quickly on summer days.

Imgiebah Bay (Selmun)

Imgiebah Bay on the Selmun side of Mellieha is a small, undeveloped bay. Plan to be self-sufficient. Bring water and shade, and check the route on the beach page before you set off.

Fomm ir-Rih Bay

Fomm ir-Rih is a remote north-west bay below clay slopes and cliffs. Plan to be self-sufficient. Go in calm weather, wear proper shoes for the path, and treat it as a swim at the end of a walk, ideally as part of a day on the coastal walking routes. Further north, the Majjistral Nature and History Park protects the coast from Golden Bay to Anchor Bay.

Rock swimming

St Peter's Pool

St Peter's Pool is a natural rock pool on the Delimara headland near Marsaxlokk, with flat limestone ledges around the water. There is no sandy beach, so bring your own shade; it gets busy in summer. Avoid jumping from the rocks, and skip swimming if the sea is rough.

Ghar Lapsi

Ghar Lapsi (Għar Lapsi) is a fishing hamlet on the south coast where people swim from the rocks. It is also a listed shore dive site, so you may see divers kitting up. Combine it with the Hagar Qim and Mnajdra temples or the Blue Grotto nearby.

In Sliema and St Julian's, long stretches of the rocky shore are used as bathing spots in summer, with ladders into the sea. They are handy if you are staying there, but conditions change quickly in a north-easterly wind.

Gozo beaches

Gozo has some of the islands' most distinctive beaches. Our Gozo travel guide covers the rest of the island.

  • Ramla Bay: Gozo's largest sandy bay, with reddish-gold sand and countryside behind it. Snack bars open in season. VisitMalta notes smooth underwater boulders a few metres out in the central strip.
  • San Blas Bay: a small red-orange sand cove at the bottom of a steep, narrow road from Nadur. The last stretch is closed to cars, so you walk down and climb back up.
  • Hondoq ir-Rummien: a cove below Qala with deep, clear water, small caves for snorkellers, ladders into the sea and a view of Comino.
  • Xlendi Bay: a mix of sand and pebbles at the head of a cliff-lined bay, shallow near the shore and close to restaurants.
  • Mgarr ix-Xini: a narrow, sheltered inlet on the south coast, popular with swimmers and divers, with a 17th-century watchtower above the entrance.

Comino

Comino is only 3.5 square kilometres and has no cars. Its beaches are reached by boat from Malta or Gozo; see Comino boat trips.

  • Blue Lagoon: the sheltered aquamarine channel between Comino and the islet of Cominotto. VisitMalta notes it is very popular with day-trippers in summer, and in July and August the small rocky shore gets packed by late morning. As of November 2026, the MTA requires a free advance booking to go ashore at the Blue Lagoon. Choose a quieter time within your booked slot. Our Comino and Blue Lagoon guide has timing advice.
  • Santa Marija Bay: one of Comino's most popular bathing spots after the lagoon, and a good escape when the lagoon is packed.

Practical tips

Most beaches are free to use, while sunbeds and umbrellas are rented by concessions on the bigger beaches. Bring water shoes for rocky entries and sea urchins, high-factor sun cream, and shade for undeveloped bays. Buses reach most of the main beaches; see getting around Malta. For snorkelling and paddling ideas, read snorkelling and stand-up paddleboarding. Check the weather before a trip to the north-west bays: wind direction decides which coast is calm.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which beach in Malta is best for young children?

Mellieha Bay is the usual choice: shallow, low-gradient sand, clear water and full facilities, and VisitMalta calls it the island's most popular family beach. Golden Bay is the alternative in the north-west, and Xlendi or Marsalforn work on Gozo.

Which Maltese beaches have Blue Flag status?

The Blue Flag is awarded each year, so the list changes. Blue Flag Malta's directory includes Mellieha Bay, Golden Bay, Ghajn Tuffieha, Bugibba Perched Beach and Ramla Bay, among others, but does not identify an award year. Confirm the award for the season you are travelling. The MTA says St George's Bay was Malta's first Blue Flag beach, in 2009.

Are there jellyfish in Malta?

Stinging jellyfish do appear at times. On managed beaches the lifeguards fly a purple flag when pests such as jellyfish are present. If you see it, stay out of the water or ask the lifeguard where it is safe to swim.

Is Ghajn Tuffieha safe for swimming?

Generally yes, but VisitMalta warns that the bay is prone to strong currents when the wind is from the north-west. The MTA defines red as high hazard and double red as water closed to the public. Ask the lifeguard before entering, and follow their instructions.

Is the Blue Lagoon worth it in summer?

The water is beautiful, but it is very crowded in July and August. Book your shore-access slot before choosing a boat, and consider visiting outside July and August for more space. Santa Marija Bay on the same island is quieter.

Does Malta have sandy beaches?

Yes, though fewer than you might expect. The main sandy beaches are in the north-west (Golden Bay, Ghajn Tuffieha, Gnejna), the north (Mellieha Bay, Armier, Paradise Bay) and on Gozo (Ramla, San Blas). Much of the coast is rock, which is excellent for snorkelling.

Which beach is best on Gozo?

Ramla Bay for space and easy sand, San Blas for a quieter cove if you can manage the steep walk, and Hondoq ir-Rummien or Mgarr ix-Xini for snorkelling and clear water.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit Malta: Month-by-Month Weather and Events
guides.summary: May, June, September and October are the best months for most visitors to Malta: a choice of sightseeing and beach weather; check actual fares and accommodation availability. Winter is mild and quiet but too cool for most swimmers.
guides.html:
The short version

Malta has a Mediterranean climate shaped by the sea around it: hot, dry and very sunny summers, a mild and fairly wet winter, and short, pleasant springs and autumns in between. Most of the year's rain falls between October and March, and from June to August it barely rains at all. Because the islands are small and close together, the weather on Gozo and Comino follows the same pattern as on Malta itself.

For most travellers the best months are May, June, September and October. Choose among these months according to your swimming preferences and the rainfall figures below. Consider winter for sightseeing and walking, and high summer for warm water and village feasts.

Malta weather by month: the figures

The table below uses two official sources. Air temperatures, rainfall and daily bright sunshine are the Malta International Airport Meteorological Office normals for Luqa for 1991 to 2020, published by the National Statistics Office in The State of the Climate 2022, Table 1.1. Rain-day counts are omitted because that table does not give them. Sea surface temperatures are the monthly climate norms quoted by the Malta Meteorological Office in its monthly weather reports; the office does not state a reference period for those sea figures, and no November value is included here.

Treat the table as a guide to the shape of the year. For the current forecast, see our Malta weather page.

Month by month

January and February: mild, green and quiet

The two coolest months bring average highs of about 16C, a sea at 15 to 16C and short winter days, with around five to seven hours of sunshine. Winter rain turns the countryside green. Consider this season for walking around Valletta, Mdina and the temple sites with indoor stops on wet days. February ends winter with Malta Carnival, listed by Festivals Malta for 5 to 9 February 2027, with floats and costumes in Valletta and a stranger, more improvised version in Nadur on Gozo. For the whole season in detail, read our Malta in winter guide.

March and April: spring flowers and Holy Week

Average highs climb from 17.4C in March to 20.1C in April, rain tails off, and daily sunshine passes eight hours by April. The sea is still cool, around 15 to 16C, so this is walking weather rather than beach weather, ideal for the cliff-top trails of the Majjistral Nature and History Park and the path along the Dingli Cliffs. Spring is also good for coastal walking and cycling on Gozo before the heat arrives. Holy Week falls in March or April; it opens on the Friday before Good Friday with a procession of Our Lady of Sorrows in Valletta and many other towns. In 2027 Good Friday is 26 March. Check school-holiday dates in your home country before booking.

May and June: the start of summer

Consider May for a mixed sightseeing and beach itinerary. Highs average 24.3C, it rarely rains, the sea reaches about 18C and the days are long. By June the average high is 28.8C, the sea is around 22C and the swimming season is in full swing at beaches such as Golden Bay, Ghajn Tuffieha Bay and Paradise Bay. The festa season begins at the end of May. Late June brings L-Imnarja, celebrated on 29 June. Check the programme for events at Buskett Gardens. Compare availability for your dates before booking.

July and August: hot, dry and busy

Peak summer is hot, with average highs above 30C, warm nights over 20C and almost no rain. The sea peaks at around 25 to 27C, which makes this the best time for snorkelling, scuba diving and boat trips to Comino. Book ahead if your travel dates fall in the summer holidays. Plan your Blue Lagoon visit and Gozo crossing in advance. The festa calendar includes the Feast of Santa Marija on 15 August, and the Malta Jazz Festival takes place in July. Plan sightseeing for early morning and evening, carry water and use the sea breeze on the north and west coasts.

September and October: warm sea, fewer people

September is still summer in all but name: average highs of 28.6C and a sea at about 26C, the warmest of the year after August. Rain starts to return, with 59.2 mm on average. The Victory Day Regatta fills the Grand Harbour on 8 September. October average highs fall to 25.0C with a sea still near 24C, and Visit Malta, the official tourism site, notes that the peak beach season can run until mid to late October. October is also a month of culture in the harbour towns: Notte Bianca lights up Valletta, and Birgufest has been held in October in Birgu, one of the Three Cities; check the next edition's programme. Rain picks up in October, with a monthly average of 77.6 mm, so pack a light waterproof.

November and December: the wet shoulder

November highs average 20.8C and the sea, still holding summer warmth, makes a swim possible on calm days. December averages 84.8 mm of rain, less than November's 89.1 mm, and sunshine falls to 5.3 hours a day. Compare prices for your dates, including the Christmas and New Year period. Christmas in Malta is a big occasion, with nativity cribs in every locality and carol services in the Baroque churches, while resort areas such as Sliema stay lively; our Malta public holidays guide lists the December holidays.

Crowds and prices through the year

Compare flight, room and car-hire quotes for your actual dates. Do not assume that a shoulder-season or winter booking will be cheaper; check cancellation terms as well as the price. If your dates are fixed to the summer holidays, book flights, rooms and any Comino or Gozo boat trip early, and consider staying outside the busiest resort areas; our where to stay in Malta guide compares the options, and Malta on a budget covers cheaper ways to travel in any season.

Festa season

The village feast, the festa, is the most Maltese thing you can see in summer. According to Visit Malta, the festa season runs as a long series of extended weekends from the end of May right through the summer and well into September, and there is hardly a weekend when some town or village is not celebrating its patron saint. A typical festa lasts three days or longer, with banners, statues and coloured festoons along the main streets, food stalls selling Maltese nougat, and evenings that often end in large ground and aerial fireworks displays. Each parish has its own date, so check the official events calendar for the weekends of your trip. Santa Marija is celebrated on 15 August; check parish programmes before travelling. The Malta International Fireworks Festival has run over several spring nights; check the next programme before choosing travel dates.

The sea-swimming season

Consider late May to late October for swimming, depending on your cold-water tolerance, when the sea sits between roughly 18C and 27C. June brings it above 20C, August and September are the warmest months in the water at around 26 to 27C, and October is still near 24C. Visit Malta's climate page notes that bathing is quite possible well into the winter months, but from December to April the sea is around 15 to 18C, too cold for most visitors to enjoy. If swimming is the point of your trip, our best beaches in Malta guide explains which bays are sandy and which are rocky, and Ramla Bay on Gozo is an option for a sandy beach day.

Which month suits which trip

  • Beach holiday: June to September, with June and September worth considering for warm water.
  • Sightseeing and history: March to May and October to November, when average highs of about 17 to 25C suit long days on foot in Valletta, the Three Cities and Mdina.
  • Walking and nature: late autumn to spring, when the countryside is green and the heat is gone.
  • Festivals: late May to mid-September for village feasts, February for Carnival, March or April for Holy Week.
  • Budget: compare actual quotes for your preferred dates.

Whenever you go, Malta's practical basics stay the same: the euro, left-hand driving, Type G three-pin plugs at 230 V and the 112 emergency number. For a first trip, start with our first-timer's guide, then pick a plan from the 7-day itinerary or the shorter 3-day itinerary.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best month to visit Malta?

For most visitors, May, June, September or October. You get warm, dry weather, a sea that is pleasant for swimming from June onwards (about 22 to 26C in June and September), and can compare dates against the rainfall table and your budget.

When is the sea warm enough to swim in Malta?

From about late May to late October. The Malta Meteorological Office gives sea temperature norms of 18.4C in May, 22.0C in June, 26.7C in August and 24.0C in October. From December to April the sea is around 15 to 18C, which most people find too cold.

How hot does Malta get in summer?

The 1991 to 2020 average highs are 31.7C in July and 32.0C in August, according to the Meteorological Office figures published by NSO. Heatwaves push temperatures past 40C on some days: in July 2023 six consecutive days reached 40C or more. Nights stay above 20C in high summer.

What is the rainiest month in Malta?

November, with 89.1 mm of rain, followed by December at 84.8 mm and January at 79.4 mm (1991 to 2020 normals). June, July and August are almost completely dry.

When is the cheapest time to visit Malta?

Compare actual room and flight prices for November to March with your other possible dates. Expect cooler weather, more rain and a sea that is too cold for most swimmers.

When is festa season in Malta?

From the end of May to well into September, with feasts on most summer weekends somewhere on Malta or Gozo. The Feast of Santa Marija falls on 15 August.

Is Malta worth visiting in winter?

Yes, if you want sightseeing, walking and quiet streets rather than beach days. Winter highs average about 16 to 17C with five to seven hours of sunshine a day, and check individual museum opening days, restaurant availability and ferry notices before travelling.

guides.title: Comino and the Blue Lagoon: Ferries, Booking, Tips
guides.summary: The Blue Lagoon now needs a free timed landing pass. How booking works, how to reach Comino, what is on the island beyond the lagoon and how to swim safely, checked in November 2026.
guides.html:
Comino sits in the channel between Malta and Gozo. VisitMalta describes it as only 3.5 square kilometres, car-free and virtually uninhabited. Its fame rests on one inlet, the Blue Lagoon, a sheltered stretch of pale turquoise water between Comino and the islet of Cominotto. The lagoon has appeared on screen many times, including in the film Swept Away and the mini-series Helen of Troy, and in summer it is a popular swimming spot.

That popularity led to a rule every visitor now needs to know: anyone stepping ashore at the Blue Lagoon must hold a free, timed landing pass. This guide explains how the system works as of November 2026, how to get to Comino, and what else the island offers. The Malta Tourism Authority states that the system caps visitors at 4,000 at any one time.

The Blue Lagoon landing pass: how booking works

The Malta Tourism Authority runs the Blue Lagoon Access Management System (AMS) on its booking portal at blcomino.com. As of November 2026, the official FAQ and booking terms set out these rules:

  • It is free. The landing pass, a QR code sent by email, costs nothing and passes are allocated first come, first served. When a slot is full, it is full.
  • You choose a time slot. The booking page offers a morning slot (08:00 to 13:30), an afternoon slot (13:30 to 17:30) and an evening slot (17:30 to 22:00). The FAQ quotes slightly shorter times (08:00 to 13:00 and 18:00 to 22:00) and explains the 30-minute difference as an allowance for boats manoeuvring in the bay.
  • Book ahead. Passes can be booked up to two months in advance. Same-day booking is possible if passes remain, but the authority advises booking well ahead.
  • Groups. One reservation covers up to four people, and the terms limit each email address to four bookings per time slot per week. Children under 5 with a parent or guardian do not need a pass.
  • No changes. Bookings cannot be modified. To cancel, the terms ask you to email the AMS in writing. A QR code can be passed to someone else as long as it has not been scanned.
  • On arrival. Staff scan your QR code before you disembark and give you a wristband. You may leave and come back within your slot, and you must hand the wristband back before you leave. Arrive early and you may be asked to wait; arrive late and you get only the time left in your slot.

The MTA's separate strategic-plan page lists 08:00 to 13:00, 13:30 to 17:30 and 18:00 to 22:00 as of November 2026; check the slot on your booking. The ferry is not included. You book and pay for your boat separately, and the AMS takes no responsibility for missed ferries or for weather cancellations. The area is not fenced, but gatekeepers patrol, and anyone ashore inside the lagoon boundary without a valid pass may be removed.

Who needs a pass, and who does not

The rule is about setting foot on land inside the Blue Lagoon area. According to the FAQ, you need a pass if you arrive by ferry, private boat or tour boat and go ashore. You do not need one to step off briefly to buy food or a drink and go straight back to the boat, or to pass through on the hard paths towards other parts of Comino without stopping in the lagoon area. Swimmers who stay on a moored tour boat do not set foot on the shore at all.

Getting to Comino

Ferries from Malta and Gozo

Comino ferries are small boats run by private operators, not by Gozo Channel. The AMS asks visitors to make sure their ferry operator is registered with Transport Malta to run to the Blue Lagoon, and links to the list of authorised vessels from its FAQ. VisitMalta's ferry listings include:

  • From Cirkewwa (Malta): Paradise Diving runs a daily ferry to the Blue Lagoon every 30 minutes from 1 May to 31 October as of November 2026, from the Paradise Bay end of Cirkewwa, near Paradise Bay.
  • From Mgarr (Gozo): Bella Comino Ferries, a family-run business based in Mgarr harbour, connects Gozo and Comino.

Comino Ferries also advertises departures from Marfa and Cirkewwa. Winter service is limited, so confirm with the operator before you set out. To reach Cirkewwa by bus, take route 41 or 42 from Valletta, 221 or 222 from Bugibba and Sliema, or the Airport Direct TD1 from the airport. Our Gozo ferry guide lists all the routes serving the Cirkewwa terminal, and the getting around Malta guide covers fares and passes.

Boat trips

Many visitors see the lagoon from a day cruise instead. Excursions leave from Sliema, St Paul's Bay and Gozo, often combining Comino's sea caves with a stop in the lagoon and sometimes a visit to Gozo. Staying on board avoids the scramble for space on the rocks, but check whether your boat provides shade. If you want to go ashore, though, you still need your own landing pass. Our Comino boat trips page compares the options, and sailing and yacht charters covers private boats.

Facilities at the Blue Lagoon

VisitMalta lists public toilets and equipment hire at the Blue Lagoon, and the AMS confirms that food and drink are sold on site. The shore is a mix of a small sandy patch and flat rock, so space for towels is tight in summer and there is little natural shade. Bring water, sun protection and shoes that can handle rock. There are no shops on Comino beyond the kiosks, so carry anything else you need from Malta or Gozo.

VisitMalta lists the Ghajnsielem Local Council in Gozo as the contact for the site.

When to go

The lagoon is at its most crowded on summer weekends and in the middle of the day, when boat trips arrive. If you are swimming, check the wind and sea conditions for your chosen slot, and the evening slot catches softer light. Early and late summer are usually less crowded than August; our best time to visit Malta guide has the month-by-month picture.

Out of season Comino is a different place. VisitMalta notes that it is worth a visit in winter for walkers and photographers, when you can smell wild thyme on the hillsides. Check that a ferry is running before you go, and see Malta in winter.

What else is on Comino

Santa Marija Bay on the north coast is the island's other main bathing spot, a sandy bay that VisitMalta calls one of the most popular on Comino. San Niklaw Bay is another beach listed by VisitMalta.

St Mary's Tower (Santa Marija Tower) stands on the high ground of the island, some 80 metres above sea level according to VisitMalta. Grand Master Alof de Wignacourt decided to build it in 1618, as part of the chain of towers linking the Cittadella in Gozo with Mdina. The square tower is about 12 metres high on an 8-metre plinth, with walls about 6 metres thick and a turret at each corner. It also appears in the film The Count of Monte Cristo. The heritage organisation Din l-Art Helwa is listed as its contact; check its opening days before you plan a visit inside.

The walks. With no cars and no towns, Comino is easy to cross on foot along its dirt tracks between the lagoon, Santa Marija Bay and the tower. The terrain is open garigue with little shade, so carry water and avoid the midday heat in summer. History adds interest along the way: VisitMalta records that the Knights kept Comino as a hunting ground after 1530, and that anyone caught breaking the hunting ban could be sentenced to three years rowing on a galley. For more walking ideas on the other islands, see coastal walking and hiking.

Below the water, Comino's coast suits snorkelling and scuba diving, and paddlers can explore the caves by sea kayak.

Safety in the water and sun

GOV.UK warns that people drown in the sea in Malta every year, that some beaches have strong undercurrents and that hidden rocks or shallow water can cause serious injury. Its advice applies fully at the Blue Lagoon:

  • Do not dive into water you do not know. The lagoon is shallow in places and the rocks edging it are uneven.
  • Swim inside the marked bathing area. Boats and other craft move constantly around the bay.
  • Learn the flags. GOV.UK notes that lifeguards patrol most beaches in summer using a flag system, and that a red flag means dangerous conditions. Take extra care when there are no lifeguards, flags or signs.
  • Follow local advice if jellyfish are present.
  • Respect the sun. Shade on the shore is scarce, so bring a hat, high-factor sunscreen and plenty of water.

In an emergency, call 112. Our emergency contacts page lists other numbers.

What to do when the slots are full

  • Try another slot or day. Passes open two months ahead, and same-day passes are released when available, so check again later or pick a weekday.
  • Stay on the boat. A boat trip lets you swim in the lagoon from the deck without going ashore.
  • Head for Santa Marija Bay. Passing through on the hard paths towards other parts of Comino does not need a pass, as long as you do not stop in the lagoon area.
  • Swim somewhere else. On Gozo, Hondoq ir-Rummien looks straight across to Comino. In northern Malta, Paradise Bay, Armier Bay and Mellieha Bay are all near Cirkewwa. Our best beaches in Malta guide has more.

Comino fits easily into a stay in Mellieha or on Gozo. See the 5-day Malta itinerary and the Gozo travel guide for where it slots in.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do you need to book to visit the Blue Lagoon in Comino?

Yes, if you want to go ashore. As of November 2026 the Malta Tourism Authority requires a free landing pass, booked online for a morning, afternoon or evening slot. You show the QR code on arrival and receive a wristband. Without a valid pass you cannot stay on land in the lagoon area.

How much does the Blue Lagoon cost?

The landing pass is free as of November 2026. You pay only for the ferry or boat trip that takes you there, which is booked separately with a licensed operator.

What are the Blue Lagoon time slots?

As of November 2026 the booking page offers 08:00 to 13:30, 13:30 to 17:30 and 17:30 to 22:00. The FAQ gives 08:00 to 13:00 and 18:00 to 22:00 for the morning and sunset slots, the 30-minute gap being an allowance for boats arriving and leaving.

Do children need a Blue Lagoon pass?

Children under 5 accompanied by a parent or guardian do not need one. Everyone else going ashore does, and one reservation covers up to four people.

Do I need a pass on a boat trip?

Only if you step onto land at the lagoon. Swimming from a moored boat does not involve going ashore. A brief stop to buy food or a drink and return straight to the boat is also exempt, according to the official FAQ.

How do I get to Comino from Malta?

Licensed ferries cross from Cirkewwa on Malta's northern tip, for example the Paradise Diving service every 30 minutes from 1 May to 31 October as of November 2026. From Gozo, Bella Comino Ferries runs from Mgarr harbour. Buses 41, 42, 221, 222 and TD1 serve Cirkewwa.

Is Comino worth visiting in winter?

Yes for walkers and photographers, as VisitMalta notes: the island is quiet, the tracks to Santa Marija Bay and St Mary's Tower are pleasant and the landscape smells of wild thyme. Ferries are much less frequent, so confirm one is running first.

guides.title: Getting Around Malta: Buses, Ferries, Taxis and Driving
guides.summary: Bus fares, Explore cards, Airport Direct routes, harbour and Gozo ferries, Bolt, Uber and eCabs, car hire and Valletta's CVA charge, with prices checked in November 2026.
guides.html:
Traffic, narrow village streets and the sea between the three islands shape every journey. There is no railway. Getting around comes down to the public bus network, a handful of ferries, taxis and ride-hailing apps, and hire cars. This guide explains each option, with fares and timetables read from the operators' own pages as of November 2026.

If you are still choosing a base, our where to stay in Malta guide matters here: staying in Valletta, Sliema or St Paul's Bay puts you on the main bus corridors, and a car-free trip becomes easy.

Public buses: fares and how to pay

Malta Public Transport runs the buses on both Malta and Gozo. You pay on board by cash, contactless bank card or phone, and a single ticket lets you change buses for free within two hours. As of November 2026 the published fares are:

TicketFare (as of November 2026)
Single journey, day routes (winter fare, 18 October 2026 to 12 June 2027)EUR 2.00
Single journey, day routes (summer fare)EUR 2.50
Night routes (numbered N)EUR 3.00
tallinja Direct routes (TD)EUR 3.00
tallinja Direct route TD1EUR 3.50

Children under 4 ride free and need no card. Inspectors do check tickets: the operator states a EUR 50 fine for passengers who cannot show a valid one, so keep your ticket or card until you step off.

tallinja cards and Explore passes

Visitors have a choice of prepaid cards, sold at Malta Public Transport sales offices and through the tallinja app. As of November 2026:

  • 12 Single Day Journeys card, EUR 19. Twelve trips on day routes with the same two-hour free transfer. It can be shared between people travelling together and stays valid for six months from first use. A night route or Airport Direct trip uses two of the twelve journeys.
  • Explore Adult, 7 days, EUR 25. Unlimited travel on day and night routes for one person, but it does not cover the tallinja Direct (TD) routes. An Explore Child card for ages 4 to 10 costs EUR 7 on the same terms.
  • Explore Flex, 4 days EUR 21 or 7 days EUR 27. Unlimited bus travel including night routes, Airport Direct and special services. The Flex card can also be topped up and used to pay for the Valletta harbour ferries, and add-on bundles include a Gozo HighSpeed return or a harbour cruise.

Which is cheapest depends on how often you ride. Two or three bus trips a day for a week makes an Explore card worthwhile; a shared 12-journey card suits a couple who mostly walk and take the odd bus. Our Malta on a budget guide sets transport against the rest of a daily budget.

From the airport: Airport Direct buses, taxis and apps

Malta International Airport at Luqa is the only airport in the country. Malta Public Transport runs limited-stop Airport Direct buses (the TD routes) from the terminal. As listed by the airport in November 2026:

  • TD1: Rabat, Bugibba, Mellieha and Cirkewwa, for Mdina and Rabat, Mellieha and the Gozo ferry.
  • TD2: St Julian's and Pembroke.
  • TD3: St Julian's, Sliema, Gzira and Msida.
  • TD4: Valletta and the Gozo fast ferry terminal.
  • TD5: Rabat and Bugibba.

The TD fare is EUR 3 (TD1 EUR 3.50) as of November 2026, paid on board. Explore Flex cards include Airport Direct, and the fares page also offers two Airport Direct trips to or from your accommodation for EUR 6. These routes replaced the old X1 to X4 airport buses in April 2025, so ignore older guides that still mention them.

The airport names Malta Taxi as the official taxi service for the islands, with a fare calculator on its site, and VisitMalta notes that taxis from the airport and the cruise terminal run on a fixed tariff to every locality. Our airport guide covers arrivals in more detail.

Night buses

Night routes carry an N prefix and cost EUR 3.00 a trip as of November 2026. The current list includes the N13 to St Julian's and the N11 and N212 to Bugibba, among others, so a late night in St Julian's does not have to end with a taxi. Night services thin out sharply outside the main resort corridor; check the route list or the tallinja app before you count on one. Special night buses are also laid on for big events such as Notte Bianca and the Malta International Fireworks Festival.

Harbour ferries: Sliema and the Three Cities

Valletta Ferry Services runs two short crossings that are quicker and calmer than the bus at rush hour. One links The Strand in Sliema with the Marsamxett side of Valletta. The other crosses the Grand Harbour between Valletta and Cospicua (Bormla), the gateway to the Three Cities, landing on the Valletta side at Lascaris Wharf next to the Barrakka Lift.

As of November 2026, on the winter timetable (1 November to 31 May), the Sliema boat leaves every 30 minutes from 06:45 until the early evening, then roughly hourly to 22:15, with extra late sailings from Friday to Sunday. The page separately lists 08:45 to 18:30 for Sundays and public holidays, despite also listing Friday-to-Sunday late trips: confirm Sunday evening departures with the operator. The Three Cities boat leaves Cospicua every 30 minutes from 06:30, and on Sundays and holidays runs 09:00 to 18:15. Summer timetables (1 June to 31 October) run later into the night.

Harbour ferry fare (as of November 2026)SingleReturn
Adult, dayEUR 3.00EUR 5.00
Child, dayEUR 1.00EUR 1.50
Adult, night service (from 19:30)EUR 3.50EUR 5.20

The ferry from Sliema is also the easy way to reach Fort St Elmo and the north side of the capital, and the Three Cities boat drops you a short walk from Fort St Angelo and the Inquisitor's Palace in Birgu. For a longer look at the harbour, see Grand Harbour cruises.

Ferries to Gozo and Comino

Two services link Malta and Gozo. Gozo Channel runs the car and passenger ferry from Cirkewwa, on Malta's northern tip, to Mgarr; the crossing takes about 25 minutes and the timetable runs around the clock as of November 2026. Gozo HighSpeed runs passenger-only catamarans from Valletta (about 45 minutes) and from Sliema via Bugibba. As of November 2026 a Gozo Channel foot passenger pays EUR 4.65 for the round trip, collected only on the Gozo side, and a standard one-way fast ferry ticket from Valletta is EUR 7.50. All the details, including car fares and how to reach Cirkewwa by bus, are in our Gozo ferry guide.

Comino is served by small licensed ferries from Cirkewwa and from Mgarr in Gozo, plus many boat trips; landing at the Blue Lagoon needs a free timed pass. Our Comino and Blue Lagoon guide explains how it works, and Comino boat trips lists the cruise options.

Taxis and ride-hailing apps

White taxis can pick you up anywhere except at bus stops, according to VisitMalta. Alongside them, three ride-hailing apps operate in Malta as of November 2026: Bolt, Uber and the Maltese company eCabs. Check the price shown in the app before you book. At busy times, compare two apps before you accept.

Car hire and driving on the left

Malta drives on the left, and VisitMalta notes that road signs are in English. More than 30 car rental companies operate from the airport, according to the airport itself. GOV.UK advises that a UK photocard licence can be used to drive in Malta; drivers from elsewhere should check with the rental company whether they also need an International Driving Permit.

GOV.UK also warns that some roads are in poor condition and that local driving standards are poor, so expect tight roundabouts, cars parked on both sides of village streets and sudden lane changes. A car pays off for exploring the west coast (Dingli Cliffs, Gnejna Bay, Golden Bay) or for a few days on Gozo, where buses are less frequent. It is a burden in Valletta, Sliema and St Julian's, where parking is scarce.

Driving into Valletta: the CVA charge

Valletta runs a Controlled Vehicular Access (CVA) system that has operated since May 2007. Cameras read number plates as vehicles enter and leave the city, and the system bills the vehicle's registered owner for the time spent inside. With a hire car that is the rental company, so check how it passes the charge on to you. As of November 2026 the tariffs published on the CVA site are:

  • Monday to Friday, 08:00 to 18:00: the first 30 minutes are free, access over 30 minutes up to 60 minutes costs EUR 0.82, and access over 60 minutes costs EUR 0.82 per hour or part thereof, capped at EUR 6.52.
  • Entering after 14:00 on a weekday: free.
  • Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays: free all day.

The simplest approach is to leave the car outside the city or come in by bus or ferry. Valletta's bus terminus sits just outside City Gate, and many routes from across the island end there.

Walking and the Barrakka Lift

Valletta is a compact grid built on a ridge, and its side streets drop steeply towards the harbour on both sides. The Barrakka Lift saves the steepest part: it rises 58 metres from Lascaris Wharf, where the Three Cities ferry lands, to the Upper Barrakka Gardens next to Castille Place in about 23 seconds.

As of November 2026 Transport Malta lists the standard fare as EUR 1 for a return on the same day, free for holders of a personalised tallinja card. Opening hours from 1 November to 30 April are 06:30 to 22:00 from Sunday to Thursday and 06:30 to 23:30 on Friday and Saturday. In summer (1 June to 30 September) the lift runs 06:30 to 00:30 daily. Gozo HighSpeed says customers buying their fast ferry ticket at the Gozo terminal receive a lift ticket.

From the top you are a few minutes' walk from St John's Co-Cathedral and the Grandmaster's Palace. Walking also works well in the lanes of Mdina and along the Sliema promenade towards St Julian's. For longer routes on foot, see coastal walking and hiking.

Putting it together

A typical car-free week looks like this: Airport Direct to your hotel, an Explore card for buses, the harbour ferry between Sliema and Valletta, a Gozo day trip by fast ferry or by bus and Gozo Channel, and an app ride for the odd late night. Hire a car only for the days you head to the west coast or around Gozo. Our 7-day Malta itinerary and the first-timer's guide show how to pace it, and the transportation planning page collects the essentials.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is a bus ticket in Malta?

As of November 2026 a single journey on a day route costs EUR 2.00 on the winter fare (18 October 2026 to 12 June 2027) and EUR 2.50 in summer. Night routes and most tallinja Direct routes cost EUR 3.00, and TD1 costs EUR 3.50. A ticket includes free transfers for two hours, and you can pay on board by cash, contactless card or phone.

Which bus goes from Malta airport to Valletta?

The Airport Direct route TD4 serves Valletta and the Gozo fast ferry terminal. It costs EUR 3 as of November 2026, or is included in an Explore Flex card. TD1, TD2, TD3 and TD5 cover Rabat, Bugibba, Mellieha, Cirkewwa, St Julian's and Sliema.

Is Uber available in Malta?

Yes. Uber, Bolt and the local company eCabs all operate in Malta as of November 2026, alongside the white taxis. Compare upfront prices in two apps at busy times.

Is it worth hiring a car in Malta?

For a stay based in Valletta, Sliema or St Julian's, usually not: buses and ferries cover the main sights and parking is hard. A car is worth it for a few days on the west coast or Gozo. Remember that Malta drives on the left and Valletta charges vehicles under its CVA system on weekday mornings.

How does parking in Valletta work?

Valletta uses Controlled Vehicular Access. As of November 2026, on weekdays between 08:00 and 18:00 the first 30 minutes are free, access over 30 minutes up to 60 minutes costs EUR 0.82, and access over 60 minutes costs EUR 0.82 per hour or part thereof, capped at EUR 6.52. Entry after 14:00 on weekdays, and all day on weekends and public holidays, is free. Cameras record the plate and the bill goes to the vehicle owner.

How much is the ferry from Sliema to Valletta?

As of November 2026 Valletta Ferry Services charges adults EUR 3.00 single or EUR 5.00 return by day, and EUR 3.50 single or EUR 5.20 return on the night service from 19:30. Children pay EUR 1.00 single. The same fares apply on the Valletta to Three Cities crossing.

How much does the Barrakka Lift cost?

Transport Malta lists the standard fee as EUR 1 for a same-day return as of November 2026, free with a personalised tallinja card. In winter it runs from 06:30 until 22:00 (23:30 on Fridays and Saturdays).

guides.title: Gozo Ferry Guide: Cirkewwa Car Ferry and Fast Ferry
guides.summary: Gozo Channel from Cirkewwa or the fast ferry from Valletta? Fares, crossing times, why you pay on the Gozo side, buses to the port and day-trip tips, checked in November 2026.
guides.html:
Getting to Gozo means crossing the Gozo Channel, and there are two ways to do it. The Gozo Channel company runs large car and passenger ferries from Cirkewwa, at the northern tip of Malta, to Mgarr harbour on Gozo. Gozo HighSpeed runs passenger-only catamarans from Valletta's Grand Harbour, and from Sliema via Bugibba, to the same harbour at Mgarr. Both are year-round services. This guide compares them, with fares and timetables read from the operators' own sites as of November 2026.

Which ferry should you take?

  • Take the Gozo Channel ferry from Cirkewwa if you are driving, staying in the north (Mellieha or St Paul's Bay), travelling late at night, or want the cheapest crossing.
  • Take the Gozo HighSpeed fast ferry if you are staying in Valletta, the Three Cities or Sliema. It saves the long bus ride to Cirkewwa, though it costs more and carries no cars.

Both land at Mgarr, a short bus ride from Victoria, the island's capital and home of the Cittadella.

The Gozo Channel ferry: Cirkewwa to Mgarr

Gozo Channel gives the crossing time as approximately 25 minutes, and the ferry runs daily. The schedule in force (3 November 2025 to 3 January 2027) runs around the clock: Gozo Channel describes a 24-hour service, subject to weather and operational conditions. Check the operator for departures on your travel date. There are no reservations: boarding is first come, first served for both cars and foot passengers, and a pre-bought ticket gives no priority.

How payment works: you pay on the Gozo side

This is the part that confuses first-time visitors. Gozo Channel tickets are round-trip tickets, and they are validated only at Mgarr in Gozo. If you start in Malta, you board at Cirkewwa without a ticket check and buy your round trip at the Mgarr terminal before you sail back. Drivers do the same: vehicles embark at Cirkewwa without validating a ticket, and pay at the Mgarr vehicle booths before the return.

You can also buy standard tickets online in advance with a debit or credit card. They are not tied to a date or sailing, are valid for six months from purchase, and must be shown individually (one printed or phone ticket per person) at Mgarr. The Mgarr passenger terminal is open 24 hours.

Gozo Channel fares (round trip)

TicketFare (as of November 2026)
Standard foot passengerEUR 4.65
Standard passenger night fare (leaving Mgarr after 20:00 and before the first morning trip, November to March)EUR 4.05
Child aged 3 to 12EUR 1.15
Infant aged 0 to 2Free (free ticket needed)
Car and driver, vehicles up to 5.3 mEUR 15.70
Car and driver night fare (leaving Mgarr after 20:00 and before the first morning trip, November to March)EUR 12.80
Motorcycle and riderEUR 8.15
BicycleEUR 1.15

The car fare covers the driver only; each passenger in the car pays the foot passenger fare. Child tickets and infants' free tickets can only be issued at the Gozo Channel booths in Mgarr, not online. Lower fares listed for Gozo residents and senior permanent residents do not apply to visitors.

The Gozo HighSpeed fast ferry from Valletta

Gozo HighSpeed sails from the Lascaris Wharf terminal on the Grand Harbour side of Valletta to Mgarr. It also runs a route from Sliema via Bugibba. According to the operator, crossings take approximately 45 minutes from Valletta, 30 minutes from Bugibba and around 1 hour 15 minutes from Sliema via Bugibba. It is a passenger-only service; bicycles travel free (up to nine per sailing), and pets are allowed.

As of November 2026 the fixed schedule shows the first departure from Valletta at 06:45 and then at 08:45, followed by hourly sailings until 22:45, with a 23:45 sailing on Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays from November to March. The first boat from Gozo to Valletta leaves at 05:45. From Sliema the first departure is 05:45, with about a dozen sailings a day.

One-way fare (as of November 2026)Valletta to GozoSliema to GozoBugibba to Gozo
Adult (standard)EUR 7.50EUR 8.50EUR 6.50
Child aged 4 to 10EUR 3.00EUR 4.00EUR 3.00
Infant up to 3FreeFreeFree

Unlike Gozo Channel, these fares are per direction, so a Valletta day return is EUR 15 for an adult. Tickets are sold online (bookings close 20 minutes before each departure) or at the terminal booths, by cash or card. If you hold an Explore Flex bus card, Malta Public Transport sells a Gozo HighSpeed return as an add-on bundle.

To reach Lascaris Wharf from the city centre, walk to the Upper Barrakka Gardens and take the Barrakka Lift down, then follow the signs. The operator says passengers travelling from Gozo get a lift ticket when the fast ferry ticket is purchased at the Gozo terminal. The Airport Direct bus TD4 also serves the fast ferry terminal, and the Valletta to Three Cities harbour ferry docks at the same wharf.

Getting to Cirkewwa by bus

Cirkewwa has its own bus terminal next to the ferry. As of November 2026, Malta Public Transport lists these routes serving it:

  • 41 and 42 to and from Valletta (41 via St Paul's Bay, Naxxar and Msida; 42 via Burmarrad, Mosta and Birkirkara).
  • 221 to Bugibba via Mellieha, and 222 to Sliema via St Paul's Bay, Bugibba and Pembroke.
  • 101 towards Mgarr (Malta) via Popeye Village, Golden Bay and Ghadira Bay.
  • X300 to Valletta via Mellieha, St Paul's Bay and Pembroke, and X299 to Mater Dei Hospital.
  • TD1 to and from Malta International Airport via Mellieha, Bugibba and Rabat.

From Valletta the bus crosses the whole island, so leave plenty of time and check the journey planner in the tallinja app. A day-route ticket costs EUR 2.00 on the winter fare as of November 2026 (EUR 3.50 on TD1). Our getting around Malta guide explains bus passes.

Buses on Gozo

Malta Public Transport also runs the Gozo network, with the same fares and cards. From Mgarr, routes 301 and 303 run to Victoria bus terminal, and route 322 runs to Marsalforn via Qala and Nadur. Victoria is the hub, and as of November 2026 the key routes from it include:

  • 310 to Marsalforn.
  • 311 to Dwejra via Gharb and San Lawrenz, for the Inland Sea at Dwejra.
  • 312 to Gharb, near the Ta' Pinu Basilica.
  • 330 to Xlendi Bay via Fontana.
  • 323 back to the ferry at Mgarr via Xewkija and Ghajnsielem.

Services on Gozo are less frequent than on the main island, so check the timetable in the tallinja app and plan your day around the bus. Gozo HighSpeed also mentions a connecting shuttle bus between Mgarr and Victoria. Alternatively, take your car across, or see cycling in Gozo.

Rough weather and disruption

The channel is short but exposed. Gozo HighSpeed states that its services may be cancelled or delayed in unfavourable sea conditions, asks passengers to check live updates on its website or social media, and does not cover the cost of alternative transport. If the fast ferry is cancelled, the Gozo Channel ferry from Cirkewwa is the usual alternative, though it can be disrupted too. Gozo Channel posts updates on its website and can be reached on +356 2210 9000. If you have a flight to catch, do not plan to return from Gozo on the morning of departure. For seasonal planning, see Malta in winter and the Malta weather page.

Tips for a Gozo day trip

  • Start early. The first fast ferry from Valletta leaves at 06:45 as of November 2026, and Gozo Channel sails through the night, so an early start buys you a full day.
  • Choose a theme. A day is enough for Victoria and the Cittadella, the Ggantija Temples and one coast, such as Ramla Bay or Dwejra, but not for all of them by bus.
  • Consider a car for Gozo only. Taking a car across costs EUR 15.70 with the driver as of November 2026, and it turns a rushed bus day into an easy loop.
  • Avoid the evening rush back. Boarding is first come, first served, so on busy summer weekends and around the Feast of Santa Marija on 15 August, drivers should allow for a wait at Mgarr.
  • Add Comino. Small ferries run to Comino from Mgarr and from Cirkewwa; see our Comino and Blue Lagoon guide.

Two or three nights on Gozo is better than a rushed day. Our Gozo travel guide and the Malta and Gozo two-week itinerary show how to split a trip, and San Blas Bay and Mgarr ix-Xini reward the extra time.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long is the ferry from Malta to Gozo?

The Gozo Channel ferry from Cirkewwa to Mgarr takes approximately 25 minutes. The Gozo HighSpeed fast ferry takes about 45 minutes from Valletta, 30 minutes from Bugibba and around 1 hour 15 minutes from Sliema via Bugibba.

Do you pay for the Gozo ferry both ways?

On Gozo Channel you pay once, for a round trip, and the ticket is validated only at Mgarr on the Gozo side. Starting from Malta, you board at Cirkewwa without a ticket and pay before your return. As of November 2026 a standard foot passenger pays EUR 4.65. The Gozo HighSpeed fast ferry charges per direction.

How much is the Gozo ferry with a car?

As of November 2026 the Gozo Channel standard fare for a car and driver (vehicle up to 5.3 metres) is EUR 15.70 for the round trip, or EUR 12.80 when leaving Mgarr after 20:00 and before the first morning trip between November and March. Each extra passenger pays the foot passenger fare.

Do I need to book the Gozo ferry?

Gozo Channel has no reservation system: boarding is first come, first served, and online tickets are not tied to a sailing. Gozo HighSpeed sells tickets online up to 20 minutes before departure and at the terminal, so booking ahead is sensible on busy days.

Does the Gozo ferry run at night?

Yes. The Gozo Channel timetable in force as of November 2026 includes sailings through the night in both directions. The last fast ferry from Valletta leaves at 22:45 from Monday to Thursday in winter, with a 23:45 sailing on Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays.

Can I take a hire car to Gozo?

Gozo Channel carries cars, and you pay the car and driver fare at Mgarr before returning. Check your rental agreement first, since some companies set conditions for taking cars off the main island.

How do I get from Valletta to the Gozo ferry?

For the fast ferry, take the Barrakka Lift down from the Upper Barrakka Gardens to Lascaris Wharf. For Cirkewwa, buses 41, 42 and X300 run from Valletta, and TD1 runs from the airport.

guides.html:
How Gozo differs from Malta

Gozo is the second island of the Maltese archipelago, a short ferry ride north-west of the main island. VisitMalta sums it up as greener, more rural and smaller than Malta, and that matches what you notice within minutes of leaving the harbour: farmland terraced behind rubble walls, villages built around a single parish church, and far less traffic than around Valletta or Sliema. Most visitors arrive by ferry. People come for prehistoric temples, sea cliffs, red-sand beaches, diving and a slower pace.

Distances are short, but a day on Gozo still rewards a plan, because the main sights sit at opposite ends of the island. Small Comino sits in the channel between the two islands and is covered in our Comino and Blue Lagoon guide.

Getting to Gozo

The main link is the Gozo Channel car ferry from Cirkewwa (Ċirkewwa) at the northern tip of Malta to Mgarr (Mġarr) harbour on Gozo. The operator gives the crossing time as approximately 25 minutes, and ferries run daily. The ticketing is unusual: you board at Cirkewwa without paying and buy or validate your ticket at Mgarr for the return journey. As of November 2026, Gozo Channel lists the standard foot passenger fare at EUR 4.65, with a cheaper night fare of EUR 4.05 for trips leaving Mgarr after 8pm and before the first morning sailing between November and March. Children aged 3 to 12 pay EUR 1.15, bought at the Gozo booths. Car and driver tickets are sold online or at the Mgarr vehicle booths only.

Gozo Highspeed also links Valletta with Mgarr, which saves the long bus ride to Cirkewwa if you are based near the capital. As of November 2026, the operator advertises 45 minutes and a standard adult or youth fare of EUR 7.50 one way. Timetables and fares for both services change by season, so check the operator's own page on the day. Our Gozo ferry guide goes through both options, and getting around Malta explains the bus routes that reach Cirkewwa. If you arrive at Malta International Airport, continue to Gozo by ferry.

Victoria and the Cittadella

All roads on Gozo lead to Victoria, which locals still call Rabat. It is the island's capital, bus hub and market town. Start in It-Tokk, the main square, then climb to the Cittadella, the walled citadel on the hill above the town that can be seen from most of the island.

The hill has been settled since prehistory, and the walls you see today are largely the work of the Knights, who rebuilt the southern flank between 1599 and 1603. Gozo suffered repeated raids, and until 1637 the island's population was required by law to spend the night inside the walls. The town below grew only once that rule was lifted. Inside, the square holds the baroque Cathedral of the Assumption (dedicated to Santa Marija), the Law Courts and the Bishop's Palace, with a cluster of small museums: the Old Prison, the Museum of Archaeology, the Gozo Nature Museum and the Gran Castello Historic House, plus a visitors' centre. As of November 2026, Heritage Malta says the Museum of Archaeology has been closed since 13 April 2026 while work proceeds on the Gozo Museum. The ramparts give a panorama across the whole island.

Heritage Malta sells a Cittadella combo ticket for its sites inside the walls. If you also plan to see Ggantija, compare the Discover Gozo combo (see below) with separate tickets. The cathedral is the focus of the Feast of Santa Marija on 15 August, one of the biggest days in the Gozitan calendar.

Ggantija Temples

The Ggantija Temples at Xaghra (Xagħra) are the reason many people cross to Gozo at all. VisitMalta dates the complex to around 3600 to 3200 BC: two temples inside a massive shared boundary wall, built from coralline limestone blocks, some over five metres long. Locals once believed only giants could have moved them, which is where the name comes from (ġgant is Maltese for giant). Ggantija is part of the Megalithic Temples of Malta, one of the country's three UNESCO World Heritage listings. The same listing includes Hagar Qim and Mnajdra and the Tarxien Temples on the main island.

As of November 2026, Heritage Malta sells Ggantija on a combined ticket with the Ta' Kola Windmill in the same village, at EUR 10 for adults. Heritage Malta has announced that the park will be closed all day on Thursday 26 November 2026, so plan around that date if you are visiting this month. Check the official opening hours page before you go, since hours change between summer and winter.

Dwejra and the Inland Sea

On the west coast, Dwejra is Gozo's most dramatic stretch of coastline. The Azure Window, the rock arch that appeared in countless photos and films, collapsed into the sea in 2017 and no longer exists. Visit Gozo now describes the site where it stood as a dive site. Dwejra is still worth the trip for what remains.

The Inland Sea is a shallow lagoon linked to open water by a tunnel through the cliff. On calm days small fishing boats take visitors out through the tunnel to see the cliffs and Fungus Rock, a stack of limestone about 60 metres high at the entrance to Dwejra Bay. The little Chapel of St Anne overlooks the lagoon. Divers come for the Blue Hole, a natural rock formation at the foot of Dwejra Point. VisitMalta describes a depth of 26 metres, with an archway opening to the sea a few metres down.

Wear proper shoes on the sharp limestone and stay back from the cliff edges, especially in wind.

Ta' Pinu Basilica

Outside the village of Gharb (Għarb) in the open countryside stands the Ta' Pinu Basilica, the national shrine and the islands' best-known place of pilgrimage. Its story begins in June 1883, when a local woman, Karmela Grima, said she heard the voice of the Virgin Mary in the old chapel that stood here. Work on the present church began in 1920 with volunteer labour from the community, and the original small chapel was built into it. Dress modestly, as at any working church. On the hill opposite, a path climbs past white marble Stations of the Cross for a view over the basilica.

Xlendi and Marsalforn

Gozo has two main seaside villages. Xlendi on the south-west coast grew from a small fishing community into a resort at the head of a narrow bay framed by cliffs. The beach mixes sand and pebbles and the water is shallow near the shore, so it suits families. Trails along the cliffs give views of the bay and the Xlendi Tower, built in 1650 to guard it, and the bay's reefs and tunnels draw divers. Read more on our Xlendi Bay page.

Marsalforn is a resort on the north coast, with a promenade, restaurants and a small sandy area sheltered by the breakwater that families use. Visit Gozo warns that the rocky swimming spots either side are for strong swimmers and should be avoided in rough weather. Walk west from Marsalforn along the coast to the salt pans near Xwejni, where sea salt is still harvested in summer.

Ramla Bay and the other beaches

Ramla Bay (Ramla l-Ħamra) is Gozo's largest sandy bay, a sweep of reddish-gold sand below terraced hills on the north coast with no hotels behind it. There are snack bars in season, and a white statue of the Virgin Mary stands on the sand. The approach from Nadur or Xaghra is the easiest. Above the bay sits Calypso's Cave, tied to the legend that Gozo was the nymph Calypso's island in Homer's Odyssey.

The other beaches each need a little effort:

  • San Blas Bay: a small red-orange sand cove reached by a steep, narrow road from Nadur. The last stretch is closed to cars, so you walk down (and back up).
  • Hondoq ir-Rummien: a cove below Qala with deep, clear water popular with snorkellers, views across to Comino, and sea access by bathing ladders.
  • Mgarr ix-Xini: a narrow, sheltered inlet on the south coast guarded by a watchtower the Knights built in 1661, popular with swimmers and divers.
  • Xlendi Bay: the easiest beach to combine with a meal, with restaurants on the waterfront.

For a full comparison with the beaches on Malta and Comino, read our guide to the best beaches in Malta.

Walking and cycling

VisitMalta describes Gozo in its entirety as excellent walking country, and the island is small enough to cover big sections on foot. Good areas include Ta' Dbiegi near San Lawrenz, the Ġordan lighthouse near Ghasri, the coast near Hondoq ir-Rummien, and the San Blas valley below Nadur. The countryside is greenest from mid-November to mid-May, which is also when walking is most comfortable. Summer heat makes midday walks hard work, and there is little shade. See coastal walking and hiking for routes across the islands.

For cyclists, VisitMalta publishes a 42 km Gozo Coastal route that starts at Ghajnsielem by Mgarr harbour and loops through Qala, Nadur, Xaghra, Marsalforn, Zebbug, Gharb, San Lawrenz, Victoria and Xewkija. Our cycling in Gozo page covers bike hire and routes. Climbers also use the sea cliffs; see rock climbing.

Diving and snorkelling

Much of Gozo's reputation abroad comes from diving: cliffs, caves, reefs and wrecks close to shore. Dwejra (the Blue Hole and the area around Fungus Rock), Xlendi and Mgarr ix-Xini are the best-known shore entries. Dive centres operate from Marsalforn, Xlendi and elsewhere. Start with our scuba diving guide, or snorkelling if you want to stay at the surface. In calm conditions sea kayaking along the cliffs is another way to see the coast.

Food to try

Gozo is known for its farm produce. Look for gbejniet, small sheep's cheeses eaten fresh, dried or peppered, and Gozitan ftira, a flat bread baked with toppings. Village restaurants serve rabbit stew, the dish many Maltese families think of first. Gozo also produces wine; see wine tasting.

How long to stay: day trip or overnight

A day trip works if you have limited time and accept that you will see only part of the island. A realistic day: early ferry, the Cittadella in the morning, Ggantija after lunch, and either Ramla Bay or Dwejra for the late afternoon. Organised tours handle the transport, which saves you working out bus connections between villages on a tight schedule.

Two or three nights change the experience. Evenings in Xlendi or Marsalforn are quiet once the day visitors have left, you can reach Dwejra or Ramla early before the boats and coaches, and you have time for a long walk or two dives. Gozo has farmhouse rentals with pools, small hotels and apartments in the resort villages; our where to stay in Malta guide compares bases on both islands. If you are building a longer trip, the 7-day itinerary and the two-week Malta and Gozo itinerary both include Gozo nights.

Practical planning

DetailInformation
FerryCirkewwa to Mgarr, about 25 minutes; foot passenger EUR 4.65 by day, paid at Mgarr (as of November 2026)
Heritage ticketsDiscover Gozo combo: EUR 13 adult, EUR 9 senior or student, EUR 7 child, valid 30 days (as of November 2026)
BusesMalta Public Transport also runs the Gozo buses; single fare EUR 2.00 in winter (as of November 2026)
Best monthsMid-November to mid-May for walking; late spring to October for swimming
Ideal stayOne full day minimum; two to three nights to see the island properly

For first-timers, our first-timer's guide to Malta and the best time to visit Malta help you fit Gozo into the wider trip.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Azure Window still standing?

No. The Azure Window at Dwejra collapsed into the sea in 2017. The site is now a dive site, and Dwejra is still worth visiting for the Inland Sea, Fungus Rock, the Blue Hole and the cliffs.

How do I pay for the Gozo ferry?

On the Gozo Channel ferry you board at Cirkewwa without a ticket and pay at Mgarr on Gozo before the return journey. As of November 2026 the standard foot passenger fare is EUR 4.65 and children aged 3 to 12 pay EUR 1.15.

Is one day enough for Gozo?

One day covers the Cittadella, Ggantija and one coastal stop such as Ramla Bay or Dwejra. To walk, dive or simply enjoy the quiet evenings, stay two or three nights.

Do I need a car on Gozo?

Not strictly. Malta Public Transport runs buses on Gozo too, but a hire car, a tour or a taxi saves time if you want to cover several sights in one day. Check the timetable before relying on a bus back to the ferry.

What does the Discover Gozo combo ticket include?

As of November 2026, Heritage Malta's Discover Gozo combo covers Ggantija Archaeological Park, Ta' Kola Windmill, the Citadel Visitor Centre, the Old Prison and the Gran Castello Historic House, valid for 30 days from first use. The adult price is EUR 13.

Which is the best beach on Gozo?

Ramla Bay is the island's largest sandy beach and the easiest choice for most visitors. San Blas is smaller and quieter but needs a steep walk, while Hondoq ir-Rummien and Mgarr ix-Xini suit snorkellers and swimmers who prefer rocky inlets.

guides.budget: Low to moderate; ferry and heritage tickets are inexpensive
