guides.html:
Planning a first trip to Malta

Malta is one of the easiest countries in Europe to visit for the first time. English is an official language, the currency is the euro, distances are short and the main sights are close together. It is also denser and busier than many first-timers expect, with traffic, construction and crowded summer beaches alongside the honey-coloured fortifications. A little planning about where you sleep and how you move around makes a big difference.

The basics to remember: Malta drives on the left, plugs are the UK-style three-pin type G at 230 volts, the international dialling code is +356 and the emergency number is 112 for ambulance, fire and police. For a quick reference of phone numbers and hospitals, see our emergency contacts page.

How the three islands fit together

The Republic of Malta is an archipelago of three inhabited islands in the central Mediterranean, south of Sicily.

  • Malta is the largest island and where almost everyone arrives. It holds the capital Valletta, the Three Cities across the Grand Harbour, the resort towns of Sliema and St Julian's, the old capital Mdina and Rabat, the northern bays around Mellieħa and St Paul's Bay, and the fishing village of Marsaxlokk in the south.
  • Gozo lies northwest of Malta, about 25 minutes away on the Gozo Channel ferry from Ċirkewwa to Mġarr. It is greener and quieter, with its own bus network and the hilltop Cittadella in Victoria.
  • Comino sits between the two and is almost uninhabited. Most people visit by boat for the Blue Lagoon.

The practical consequence: everything on Malta island is reachable in a day trip from any base, and Gozo works as a day trip too, but each ferry crossing adds time at both ends. Our Gozo ferry guide explains the car ferry and the fast ferry from Valletta.

How many days do you need?

  • 3 days: Valletta and the Three Cities, the temples or the Hypogeum, and Mdina. See the 3-day itinerary.
  • 5 days: add a beach day in the north and a day trip to Gozo. See the 5-day itinerary.
  • 7 days or more: time for Comino, a night or two on Gozo, walks along the cliffs and slower days. See the 7-day itinerary or the two-week Malta and Gozo itinerary.

Malta is a year-round destination. Summer is hot and crowded, spring and autumn are better for walking and sightseeing, and winter is mild but can be wet and windy. Our best time to visit Malta guide and the weather page go month by month.

Where to base yourself

For a first trip, pick one base on Malta island and add Gozo as a day trip or a short second stay.

  • Valletta for history, evening walks and the best transport links.
  • Sliema for a seafront promenade, shops and the ferry across to Valletta.
  • St Julian's for restaurants and nightlife, with Paceville at its loud end.
  • St Paul's Bay, Bugibba and Qawra or Mellieħa for the northern beaches and the Gozo ferry.

The full comparison, with trade-offs for each area, is in our where to stay in Malta guide.

Getting from the airport

Malta has one airport, Malta International Airport (MLA) at Luqa, in the south of the main island. There is no airport on Gozo for scheduled flights, so everyone heading to Gozo continues by road and ferry.

As of November 2026, Malta Public Transport lists these Airport Direct buses from the bus terminal outside arrivals:

  • TD1: Rabat, Buġibba, Mellieħa and Ċirkewwa (for the Gozo ferry), hourly.
  • TD2: St Julian's and Pembroke, every 30 minutes.
  • TD3: St Julian's, Sliema, Gżira and Msida, every 30 minutes.
  • TD4: Valletta and the Gozo fast ferry, every 30 minutes.
  • TD5: Rabat and Buġibba, hourly.

As of November 2026, Malta Public Transport lists the Airport Direct fare at €3 per passenger, or €3.50 on TD1, paid in cash or by contactless card on board, with no booking needed. Check the tallinja app for current timetables. Taxis and pre-booked transfers are also available outside arrivals. For buses, ferries and driving across the islands, see getting around Malta and our transport planning page.

Entry rules

Malta is a member of the European Union and of the Schengen area. EU citizens travel on a passport or national ID card; most other visitors follow the Schengen short-stay rules. Requirements depend on your nationality, so check our visa requirements page and your own government's advice before booking.

Two EU systems are worth knowing about as of November 2026:

  • Entry/Exit System (EES): the European Commission states that the EES became fully operational on 10 April 2026. Travellers covered by EES register biometric details at the external Schengen border. Exemptions apply, and children under 12 do not have fingerprints scanned, so check the rules for your situation and allow extra time at passport control.
  • ETIAS: the European Commission ETIAS page states that ETIAS is not yet in operation and that no applications are being collected. The EU says it will announce the start date several months before launch. Ignore any website that asks you to pay for an ETIAS today.

Money and costs

Malta uses the euro. Cards and contactless payments are widely accepted in shops, restaurants and on buses, and ATMs are easy to find in towns and at the airport. Keep some small change for kiosks selling pastizzi, village feasts and the occasional cash-only bar. Prices rise in July and August and in the busiest resort areas. For ways to keep costs down, read Malta on a budget.

Visitors aged 18 and over in licensed accommodation also pay the environmental contribution, collected by the accommodation. As of November 2026, the Malta Tourism Authority lists it at €1.50 per person per night since 1 July 2026, capped at €22.50 per person per visit. Rates are set by national budget measures and can change, so check what your booking includes.

Tipping is a personal choice. Check your bill first to see whether a service charge has been added. One specific case: Visit Malta notes that public car parks managed by Transport Malta are free to use and that tipping the attendants is optional.

Language

Maltese and English are official languages. Signs, menus and public transport information are in English, so first-timers rarely have trouble. Maltese is a Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet, which explains place names such as Ħaġar Qim and Għajn Tuffieħa. Learning grazzi (thank you) and bongu (good morning) is a friendly touch.

Driving on the left

Malta drives on the left, unlike most of Europe. Visit Malta gives speed limits of 60 to 80 km/h on open roads and 30 to 50 km/h in villages and built-up areas unless signs say otherwise, and notes that the alcohol limit for drivers is low and that using a mobile phone at the wheel is heavily penalised. Car hire companies set their own age rules; Visit Malta states that renters must be over 21 and under 70, and drivers under 25 may pay a surcharge. UK visitors can drive on a photocard licence, according to the UK government's travel advice.

Do you need a car? Not for Valletta, Sliema or St Julian's, where traffic and parking are hard work and buses and ferries cover most trips. A car helps on Gozo and for reaching quieter bays and cliff walks. Satellite navigation sometimes picks narrow rural lanes, especially on Gozo, so use judgement before following it down a farm track.

Plugs, water and health

  • Plugs: Malta uses UK-style three-pin type G plugs, at 230 volts and 50 hertz. Bring an adaptor if your devices use another plug.
  • Tap water: the Water Services Corporation says Malta's tap water continues to exceed the strictest European standards for safety and taste. Some people find the taste mineral, so many locals and visitors still buy bottled water. A filter bottle is a good compromise.
  • Healthcare: EU visitors should carry an EHIC and UK visitors a GHIC, plus travel insurance. Pharmacies are common in every town.
  • Sun: summer heat is strong and shade is scarce on rocky beaches. Carry water and plan sightseeing for mornings and late afternoons.

Common first-timer mistakes

  • Booking the Hypogeum too late. Heritage Malta strongly recommends booking early because visitor numbers are limited, so reserve as soon as your dates are fixed.
  • Arriving at the Blue Lagoon without a slot. Since May 2025, visitors arriving by boat who wish to go ashore at the Blue Lagoon need a free online booking for one of three daily time slots. Read our Comino and Blue Lagoon guide.
  • Underestimating journey times. Distances are short but roads are congested, and a bus ride across the island can take longer than the map suggests.
  • Treating Gozo as a quick hop. Add the drive or bus to Ċirkewwa, the queue and the crossing. Our Gozo travel guide helps you decide between a day trip and an overnight stay.
  • Expecting long sandy beaches everywhere. Most of the coast is rock. Sandy bays such as Golden Bay and Mellieħa Bay fill early in summer; see the best beaches in Malta.
  • Skipping the ferries. The ferry rides from Valletta to Sliema and to the Three Cities avoid road traffic and give harbour views.
  • Letting your guard down in Paceville. The UK government's travel advice warns of drink spiking in some bars there. Buy your own drinks, keep them in sight and check your bill.

For more on etiquette and daily life, see our local tips, then browse things to do in Malta to start filling your days.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a visa to visit Malta?

Malta is in the EU and the Schengen area, so EU citizens travel on a passport or national ID card and most other visitors follow Schengen short-stay rules. Requirements depend on your nationality, so check our visa requirements page and your own government's advice. As of November 2026, the EU Entry/Exit System is fully operational, while ETIAS is not yet in operation.

Do I need ETIAS for Malta?

Not yet. As of November 2026, the European Commission ETIAS page says ETIAS is not in operation and no applications are being collected. The EU will announce the start date several months before launch, so check the official site closer to your trip and avoid unofficial sites that charge for applications.

How do I get from Malta airport to my hotel?

Malta International Airport (MLA) at Luqa is served by Malta Public Transport's Airport Direct buses: TD1 to Rabat, Buġibba, Mellieħa and Ċirkewwa; TD2 to St Julian's and Pembroke; TD3 to St Julian's, Sliema, Gżira and Msida; TD4 to Valletta; and TD5 to Rabat and Buġibba. As of November 2026 the fare is €3, or €3.50 on TD1. Taxis are available outside arrivals.

Does Malta drive on the left?

Yes. Malta drives on the left, unlike most of Europe. Visit Malta gives limits of 60 to 80 km/h on open roads and 30 to 50 km/h in built-up areas unless signed otherwise. The drink-driving limit is low and mobile phone use at the wheel is heavily penalised.

Is tap water safe to drink in Malta?

The Water Services Corporation says Malta's tap water exceeds the strictest European standards for safety and taste. Many people still prefer bottled or filtered water because of the taste.

What plugs does Malta use?

Malta uses the UK-style three-pin type G plug at 230 volts and 50 hertz. Bring an adaptor if your devices use a different plug.

Do people speak English in Malta?

Yes. English and Maltese are both official languages. Signs, menus and transport information are in English.

Should I tip in Malta?

Tipping is a personal choice. Check whether a service charge is already on the bill before adding anything. Tipping attendants at the free public car parks run by Transport Malta is optional.

How many days do I need in Malta?

Three days covers Valletta, the Three Cities, Mdina and one prehistoric site. Five days adds a beach day and a Gozo day trip. A week or more gives time for Comino, a night on Gozo and some coastal walks.

guides.summary: Malta in winter is mild and quiet, with average highs of about 16 to 17C, five to seven hours of sunshine a day and winter rain. Sightseeing, walking and festivals beat beach time.
guides.html:
The short version

Winter in Malta runs from December to February and is mild by northern European standards. Daytime highs average about 16 to 17C, average lows sit around 10 to 12C, and the sun still shines for around five to seven hours a day. It is also the wettest part of the year, with December averaging 84.8 mm of rain and January 79.4 mm. The sea cools to about 15 to 18C, too cold for most visitors.

That makes winter a season for history, food, walking and festivals rather than beaches. Plan museum visits, meals and ferry trips around individual opening days and service notices, and compare actual room quotes. If you can live without a swim, it is one of the most rewarding times to see the islands.

Winter weather in figures

Air temperatures, rainfall and daily bright sunshine below are the Malta International Airport Meteorological Office normals for Luqa for 1991 to 2020, published by the National Statistics Office in The State of the Climate 2022, Table 1.1. That table does not give rain-day counts. Sea temperatures are separate monthly norms quoted by the Malta Meteorological Office in its reports; those reports do not specify the sea reference period.

MonthAverage highAverage lowRainfallSunshine per daySea temperature
December17.1C (63F)11.8C (53F)84.8 mm5.3 hours18.3C (65F)
January15.7C (60F)10.0C (50F)79.4 mm5.4 hours15.8C (60F)
February15.7C (60F)9.6C (49F)68.9 mm6.6 hours15.3C (60F)

A few things these averages do not show. November has the highest monthly rainfall average in the 1991 to 2020 table, at 89.1 mm, followed by December at 84.8 mm. Keep an indoor option for stormy days. Allow for wind as well as temperature: a cold northerly or north-easterly makes 15C feel much cooler on an exposed bastion or ferry deck, as Visit Malta notes when it describes winter's occasional short cold spells. Monthly averages do not rule out warmer water: the Meteorological Office recorded 20.5C in December 2024, 2.2C above the sea norm quoted in that report. Check the forecast on our Malta weather page the week before you fly.

Month by month

December: Christmas season

December starts with the Feast of the Immaculate Conception on 8 December and Republic Day on 13 December, both public holidays, and builds towards Christmas. The separate sea norm quoted for December is 18.3C, warm enough for a short swim on a calm, sunny day if you are used to cold water. Days are the shortest of the year, so plan outdoor sightseeing for the morning and early afternoon.

January: a sightseeing month

After New Year's Day, compare accommodation quotes and check the opening notices for the sites you want to visit. Average highs are about 16C, monthly rainfall averages 79.4 mm, and the countryside turns green. It is the best month to see the major sites with room to breathe, from St John's Co-Cathedral to the Hal Saflieni Hypogeum, which still needs booking well ahead.

February: Carnival and longer days

February is a little drier and brighter than January, with 6.6 hours of bright sunshine a day. The Feast of St Paul's Shipwreck on 10 February is a public holiday, and Carnival falls in the days before Ash Wednesday. Festivals Malta has published 5 to 9 February for Carnival 2027.

What is open in winter

Malta does not shut down for winter the way some Mediterranean resort islands do. Valletta, Sliema, St Julian's and the main towns are working cities all year, and most restaurants, cafes and hotels stay open.

  • Museums and sites. Heritage Malta runs its museums and sites through the winter and closes on 1 January, Good Friday and 24, 25 and 31 December. That covers the National Museum of Archaeology, Fort St Elmo and the National War Museum, Hagar Qim and Mnajdra and the Ggantija Temples on Gozo. As of November 2026, Heritage Malta also lists a Hypogeum closure from 18 to 24 January 2027. Check current hours and special notices before you go.
  • Buses. Malta Public Transport runs all year, with holiday changes. Its December 2025 notice announced lunchtime suspensions and an early finish on Christmas Day and New Year's Day; check the new notice for your travel dates. See our getting around Malta guide.
  • Gozo ferry. The Gozo Channel car and passenger ferry between Cirkewwa and Mgarr runs all winter. On Christmas Day and New Year's Day it has paused for a few hours around lunchtime in recent years. Rough weather can delay or cancel smaller boats, so keep plans flexible. Details are in our Gozo ferry guide.
  • The airport. Malta International Airport operates all year, though some seasonal routes do not fly in winter, so check direct connections from your home airport.

Christmas in Malta

Christmas is a major celebration on both islands, as much a religious feast as a social one. Visit Malta describes cribs as "positively everywhere", from private houses to small chapels, and touring the cribs, called presepju in Maltese, is a popular local pastime. Some are large, detailed scenes with moving figures built by local craftsmen. Parish churches are decorated for Advent, and Visit Malta recommends the candlelit carol singing at St John's Co-Cathedral in Valletta for a memorable evening. The annual Christmas pantomime at the Manoel Theatre in Valletta mixes slapstick for children with satire for adults.

On Gozo, the big seasonal draw is Bethlehem f'Ghajnsielem (Betlehem f'Għajnsielem), a live, walk-through nativity village. Visit Gozo's historical description records more than 20,000 square metres at Ta' Passi, with an inn, a bakery, a carpenter's workshop, a working farm and more than 150 actors. These are historical details, not a confirmed 2026 cast or layout. Opening days and times are announced each year, so check before you plan a Gozo day around it. Visit Gozo also notes guided crib tours through Gozo's villages during December. Combine a visit with a night in Victoria or Xlendi and a walk up to the Cittadella.

Remember that Heritage Malta sites close on 24, 25 and 31 December and 1 January, and that in 2026 Christmas Day falls on a Friday and New Year's Day 2027 on a Friday too. Our Malta public holidays 2027 guide lists every date.

Carnival in February

Malta Carnival is the highlight of late winter. Visit Malta describes a carnival week of brightly coloured floats on lorries, children in fancy dress and late-night parties in Paceville, the nightlife district of St Julian's. The main action is in Valletta, with local versions in towns and villages across the islands. For something different, go to Nadur on Gozo, where Visit Malta says carnival takes on "a more macabre and funny mood". Festivals Malta has published 5 to 9 February for the 2027 edition. Look out for imqaret, fried date-filled pastries, as a snack while you watch.

Winter is walking season

From late autumn to spring the islands are green, the light is clear and the heat that makes summer hiking hard is gone. This is the best time of year for coastal walking and hiking. Good winter routes include:

  • The cliff tops and valleys of the Majjistral Nature and History Park in the north-west, above Golden Bay and Ghajn Tuffieha Bay.
  • The edge of the Dingli Cliffs, combined with the woodland of Buskett Gardens and the old town of Mdina and Rabat.
  • The south-east coast around Marsaxlokk and the Xrobb l-Ghagin Nature Park, finishing with a fish lunch by the harbour.
  • On Gozo, the coast at Dwejra and the lanes between villages, which also suit cycling on routes chosen for your experience.

Winter also suits birdwatching at the wetland reserves of Ghadira and Simar; check the managing organisation's opening days before you go. Carry water and a layer even on sunny days, and avoid cliff edges in strong wind.

What not to expect

  • Beach days. A sea at 15 to 16C in January and February is bracing, not relaxing. You can sit on a beach in the sun on a calm day, but do not plan a winter trip around swimming. If the sea matters, the best time to visit Malta guide explains when it warms up.
  • Reliable boat trips. Fewer excursion boats run in winter, and crossings to the Blue Lagoon and Comino depend on the sea state. Treat a Comino boat trip as a bonus on a calm day.
  • Long evenings outdoors. Days are short and evenings cool, so dinners move indoors. Café terraces in the sun are still pleasant at midday.
  • Summer festas. The extended village festa season runs from late May into September, according to Visit Malta. Winter also has its own feast days, Christmas and Carnival.

What to pack

  • Layers: T-shirts for sunny afternoons, a warm jumper or fleece for evenings, and a windproof jacket for bastions, cliffs and ferry decks.
  • A compact umbrella or a light waterproof: bring one for winter rain.
  • Walking shoes with grip: limestone paths and old stone streets get slippery when wet.
  • Sunglasses and sunscreen: winter sun in Malta is still strong at midday.
  • A swimsuit only if you are a cold-water swimmer, or your hotel has a heated pool.
  • A Type G (UK-style, three-pin) plug adapter if you are coming from outside the UK or Ireland; the supply is 230 V.

For a first winter visit, a week split between Valletta and Gozo works well: see our 5-day itinerary or the 7-day itinerary, and the Malta on a budget guide for comparing costs. The emergency number in Malta is 112; see our emergency contacts page.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Malta warm in winter?

Mild rather than warm. Average daytime highs are 17.1C in December and 15.7C in January and February (Meteorological Office Luqa normals for 1991 to 2020, published by NSO), with lows around 10 to 12C. Sunny afternoons can feel warm out of the wind, but evenings are cool.

Can you swim in Malta in winter?

Only if you like cold water. The Malta Meteorological Office gives sea temperature norms of 18.3C in December, 15.8C in January and 15.3C in February. Most visitors find it too cold.

Does it rain a lot in Malta in winter?

Winter is the wettest season. December averages 84.8 mm of rain, January 79.4 mm and February 68.9 mm (1991 to 2020 normals). Average daily bright sunshine is 5.3, 5.4 and 6.6 hours respectively; rainfall totals do not tell you how many days will be wet.

Is everything closed in Malta in winter?

No. Check individual businesses and service notices for your dates. Heritage Malta museums and sites close on 24, 25 and 31 December and 1 January (and on Good Friday), but individual sites can have additional closures. As of November 2026, the Hypogeum is also scheduled to close from 18 to 24 January 2027. Fewer excursion boats run, and sea trips depend on the weather.

When is Carnival in Malta in 2027?

Festivals Malta lists Carnival 2027 on 5 to 9 February, just before the Feast of St Paul's Shipwreck on 10 February. The main events are in Valletta, with a distinctive local carnival in Nadur on Gozo. Check the official programme closer to the date for exact times.

What is Christmas like in Malta?

Christmas is a major religious and social festival. Expect nativity cribs everywhere, carol services in the parish churches including a candlelit service at St John's Co-Cathedral, the Christmas pantomime at the Manoel Theatre, and the live nativity village of Bethlehem f'Ghajnsielem on Gozo.

Is winter a good time to visit Gozo?

Yes, for walking, cycling and quiet villages. The ferry runs all year, Gozo is at its greenest, and December brings the Bethlehem f'Ghajnsielem nativity village. Pack for wind and rain, and keep a spare day in case rough seas disrupt plans.

guides.title: Malta on a Budget: Buses, Passes, Cheap Eats and Free Sights
guides.summary: Malta on a budget works if you ride the buses, buy the right heritage pass, swim at free beaches, eat pastizzi and ftira, travel outside July and August, and base yourself where cheap rooms cluster.
guides.html:
Malta is small, uses the euro, and packs a lot into short distances, which makes it easier to do cheaply than many Mediterranean islands. You do not need a hire car for most trips, a lot of the best sights cost nothing, and local snacks can help keep food costs down. This guide covers the decisions that save the most money, with prices only where we read them on the official page in November 2026.

When to go: avoid July and August

Timing is the biggest lever on your budget. July and August are busy summer months, so compare flight and room prices against other dates. Consider the shoulder months, roughly April to June and late September to October, and check sea conditions before planning swims. VisitMalta notes that beach life lasts well into October.

Winter can suit a budget trip focused on city sightseeing, walking and museums, though the sea is cool for most visitors. From mid-November to mid-May the countryside turns green, which is when the walking is at its best. Read Malta in winter and best time to visit Malta to pick your dates, and check Malta public holidays 2027 before booking, since holiday weekends fill rooms fast.

Getting around: buses, not taxis or hire cars

Malta Public Transport runs the bus network on Malta and Gozo, and for most visitors it is the cheapest way around. As of November 2026, its fares page lists:

  • Single journey, winter: EUR 2.00 on day routes, valid for two hours, from 18 October 2026 to 12 June 2027.
  • Single journey, summer: EUR 2.50 on day routes.
  • Night routes: EUR 3.00.
  • 12 Single Day Journeys card: EUR 19 for 12 journeys, with free transfers within two hours. It can be shared and is valid for six months from first use.
  • Children: under-4s travel free and need no card.

You can pay for a single on board by cash, contactless card or phone. The 12-journey card brings the cost per trip well below the summer single fare and can be shared between two people travelling together. If you plan to ride several times a day, look at the Explore cards, which give unlimited bus travel for a set number of days. As of November 2026, Explore Adult 7 Day costs EUR 25, while the separate Explore Flex seven-day bus offer costs EUR 27. Explore Adult covers day and night routes and selected special services, excluding tallinja Direct routes. The Flex offer also lists Airport Direct. Both are for individual use. Explore Flex can be bought at a sales office or ticket machine and added to the tallinja app, where you can top it up with a credit card.

Taxis and ride-hailing add up quickly, and parking in Valletta, Sliema and St Julian's is hard work, so a hire car rarely saves money unless you are touring Gozo or travelling as a group. Our getting around Malta guide and the transport planning page cover routes and the airport bus from Malta International Airport.

The Gozo ferry is cheap

A trip to Gozo costs less than many visitors expect. As of November 2026, Gozo Channel lists the standard foot passenger fare at EUR 4.65, paid at Mgarr on Gozo before you sail back, with a lower night fare of EUR 4.05 for departures from Mgarr after 8pm and before the first morning trip between November and March. Children aged 3 to 12 pay EUR 1.15. See our Gozo ferry guide and Gozo travel guide.

Free and low-cost sights

Many of Malta's best experiences cost nothing:

  • Walk Valletta. The whole of Valletta is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its streets, bastions and harbour views are free. The Upper Barrakka Gardens, a public garden since 1824, has one of the best views of the Grand Harbour and the Three Cities.
  • Explore Mdina. The walled city of Mdina is free to wander, and its lanes are quietest early in the morning or in the evening.
  • The Gozo Cittadella. On Gozo, walking up to the Cittadella and around its ramparts gives a view across the whole island. The museums inside are ticketed.
  • Clifftops and countryside. Dingli Cliffs, Dwejra on Gozo and the Majjistral Nature and History Park are open landscapes you can walk for free. See coastal walking and hiking.
  • Marsaxlokk on a Sunday. The Sunday fish market at Marsaxlokk, among the colourful luzzu fishing boats, costs nothing to browse.
  • Beaches. Public beaches are free; you pay only if you rent a sunbed. Our best beaches in Malta guide covers sandy bays and free rock swimming spots such as St Peter's Pool.
  • Village festas. Summer village feasts bring fireworks, processions and sweet street food to the villages, and watching costs nothing. Big dates include the Feast of Santa Marija on 15 August; check the events calendar for Notte Bianca and other free street events.

Heritage Malta passes: which one to buy

Heritage Malta runs most state museums and archaeological sites, and it sells passes that cut the cost if you plan several visits. As of November 2026, its online store lists:

  • Heritage Malta Multisite Pass: EUR 60 adult, EUR 45 senior, EUR 45 student, EUR 30 child, valid for 30 days from first use. The store says it also covers the Grandmaster's Palace, the Cittadella Visitors' Centre and the Malta National Aquarium, but it is NOT valid for the Hal Saflieni Hypogeum or Valletta Underground.
  • Family Multisite Pass: EUR 130.
  • Discover Gozo Combo: EUR 13 adult, EUR 9 senior or student, EUR 7 child, covering Ggantija, the Ta' Kola Windmill, the Citadel Visitor Centre, the Old Prison and the Gran Castello Historic House, valid 30 days.
  • Single-area combos such as the Valletta Combo, the Harbour Combo, the Rabat Combo, the Prehistoric Combo and Hagar Qim and Mnajdra.

The Multisite Pass makes sense if you will visit many paid sites over a week or more. Heritage Malta publishes a brochure listing every site it covers; check it against your own list, which might include the Grandmaster's Palace, Fort St Elmo and the National War Museum, the National Museum of Archaeology, Hagar Qim and Mnajdra, Fort St Angelo and the Ggantija Temples. For a short trip, add up the individual or combo tickets for the sites you will actually see; a combo often wins. The Hypogeum is excluded from the pass and needs its own ticket, so book it early. St John's Co-Cathedral sells its own tickets too.

Eat like a local

Street food is where Malta is cheapest. Pastizzi, savoury pastries filled with ricotta, are sold hot from small pastizzerias and are the classic cheap snack. Ftira and hobz biz-zejt (crusty bread rubbed with tomato and topped with sheep's cheese, anchovies and olive oil) make a filling beach lunch. Imqaret, date pastries, turn up at village festas, and Gozitan gbejniet cheese can be found at markets and grocers.

Other ways to cut food costs:

  • Shop at supermarkets and grocers for picnics, especially for beach days.
  • Choose a room with a kitchen if you are staying a week or more.
  • Compare lunch menus with dinner prices before deciding where to eat.
  • Drink tap water only if your accommodation confirms it is fine; otherwise large bottles from a supermarket are far cheaper than small ones from beach kiosks.

For a taste of traditional cooking without restaurant prices, our food tours and cooking classes page lists options, and the dishes hub explains what to order.

Where budget rooms cluster

Your base affects both the room rate and your bus budget. VisitMalta's hostel listing includes properties in Sliema, Gzira, Msida and St Julian's, as well as Marsalforn on Gozo and Valletta. These harbour towns also have many small guesthouses and self-catering flats, and good bus connections to Valletta and the rest of the island.

St Paul's Bay, which includes Bugibba and Qawra, is Malta's largest seaside resort area and has a wide spread of apartments and mid-range hotels, with buses towards the northern beaches and the Gozo ferry. Valletta can cost more per night, but it saves on transport if you will spend most days sightseeing there. On Gozo, compare apartments in Marsalforn and Xlendi with farmhouse rentals with pools. Compare areas in where to stay in Malta.

Sample budget-minded itineraries

A focused trip costs less than one that tries to see everything. A five-day itinerary covers Valletta, Mdina and a Gozo day trip by bus and ferry, while the seven-day plan adds beaches and walks with free entry. Read local tips for everyday advice and our first-timer's guide for the basics.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is a bus ticket in Malta?

As of November 2026, Malta Public Transport charges EUR 2.00 for a single on day routes in winter (18 October 2026 to 12 June 2027), EUR 2.50 in summer and EUR 3.00 on night routes. A single is valid for two hours.

Is the 12 Single Day Journeys card worth it?

For most visitors, yes. As of November 2026 it costs EUR 19 for 12 journeys, includes free transfers within two hours, can be shared, and stays valid for six months from first use. It is cheaper per journey than buying singles.

Is the Heritage Malta Multisite Pass worth buying?

Only if you will visit many paid Heritage Malta sites within 30 days. As of November 2026 it costs EUR 60 for adults and excludes the Hypogeum and Valletta Underground. For a short trip, a combo ticket such as the Valletta Combo or the Discover Gozo Combo is often better value.

What are the cheapest things to eat in Malta?

Pastizzi from a pastizzeria, ftira or hobz biz-zejt from a bakery, and picnic food from supermarkets. Compare menus before choosing a sit-down meal.

What is the cheapest time to visit Malta?

Compare winter dates outside Christmas, New Year and Carnival with the shoulder months, April to June or late September to October. Prices depend on your dates and accommodation, and swimming conditions vary.

Can I visit Gozo cheaply?

Yes. As of November 2026 a foot passenger on the Gozo Channel ferry pays EUR 4.65 by day, and the Discover Gozo combo ticket covers five heritage sites for EUR 13 (adult). Ride the bus to Cirkewwa and use Gozo's buses on the island.

Where should I stay in Malta on a budget?

Look for hostels and guesthouses in Sliema, Gzira, Msida and St Julian's, with good buses. St Paul's Bay (Bugibba and Qawra) has a large supply of apartments. On Gozo, look at Marsalforn and Xlendi.

guides.title: Malta Public Holidays 2027: Full List with Dates and Weekdays
guides.summary: Malta has 14 public holidays in 2027: five national holidays and nine other public holidays set by law. Good Friday falls on 26 March, and three holidays land on a weekend without a substitute weekday.
guides.html:
The short version

Malta and Gozo share one calendar of 14 public holidays a year. Five of them are national holidays tied to the country's modern history, and nine are public holidays, most of them Catholic feast days. All 14 are set by the National Holidays and Other Public Holidays Act (Chapter 252 of the Laws of Malta). Thirteen fall on a fixed date every year. The only movable one is Good Friday, which in 2027 falls on Friday 26 March, two days before Easter Sunday on 28 March.

For a visitor, a public holiday in Malta rarely spoils a trip. Government offices close by law, and the state museums run by Heritage Malta close on a short list of days, but beaches, most restaurants in the tourist areas, buses and the Gozo ferry keep going. What changes is the mood: several of these dates are the biggest days in the island's religious and festive calendar, and they are worth planning around rather than avoiding.

Malta public holidays 2027: the full list

The table below follows the order of the year. Weekdays are calculated for 2027. "National" marks the five national holidays listed in article 2 of the Act; the rest come from the Schedule to the Act.

DateWeekdayHolidayType
1 January 2027FridayNew Year's DayPublic holiday
10 February 2027WednesdayFeast of St Paul's ShipwreckPublic holiday
19 March 2027FridayFeast of St JosephPublic holiday
26 March 2027FridayGood FridayPublic holiday
31 March 2027WednesdayFreedom Day (Jum il-Ħelsien)National holiday
1 May 2027SaturdayWorkers' DayPublic holiday
7 June 2027MondaySette GiugnoNational holiday
29 June 2027TuesdayFeast of St Peter and St Paul (L-Imnarja)Public holiday
15 August 2027SundayFeast of the Assumption (Santa Marija)Public holiday
8 September 2027WednesdayVictory Day (Jum il-Vittorja), Feast of Our Lady of VictoriesNational holiday
21 September 2027TuesdayIndependence Day (Jum l-Indipendenza)National holiday
8 December 2027WednesdayFeast of the Immaculate ConceptionPublic holiday
13 December 2027MondayRepublic Day (Jum ir-Repubblika)National holiday
25 December 2027SaturdayChristmas DayPublic holiday

Two common assumptions do not apply in Malta. Easter Monday and Boxing Day are not separately named public holidays in Malta. In 2027, however, 26 December falls on a Sunday and is therefore a public holiday under the Sunday rule. Every Sunday is also a public holiday under the same Act, which is why Easter Sunday does not appear in the list.

Good Friday 2027: why 26 March

Malta follows the Western (Gregorian) church calendar, so Good Friday is the Friday before Western Easter Sunday. In 2027 Easter Sunday is 28 March, which puts Good Friday on 26 March. That creates an unusual cluster in late March 2027: St Joseph on Friday 19 March, Good Friday on Friday 26 March and Freedom Day on Wednesday 31 March, three public holidays in under two weeks.

Holy Week is one of the most striking times to be in Malta. Good Friday processions take place in many towns and villages, and the days around Easter bring their own food and church traditions. Our guide to Holy Week and Easter in Malta covers what to see. Note that Heritage Malta closes all its museums and sites on Good Friday, so leave the temples and state museums for another day, and check the hours of churches such as St John's Co-Cathedral before you go, since services take priority during Holy Week.

What happens when a holiday falls on a weekend

Malta does not move a public holiday to the following Monday. The holiday stays on its date. What the law changed is the effect on workers: under article 6(c) of the Act, with effect from 1 January 2021, when a national or public holiday falls on a Saturday or Sunday it counts for "entitling any person to a day of vacation leave in addition to the leave entitlement" for that year. In other words, employees get an extra day of leave to take later, not a bank-holiday Monday.

In 2027 three holidays fall on a weekend:

  • Workers' Day, Saturday 1 May
  • Feast of the Assumption, Sunday 15 August
  • Christmas Day, Saturday 25 December

No substitute public holiday is created on Monday 3 May, Monday 16 August or Monday 27 December. Individual businesses may still choose to close.

What closes on a public holiday

Government offices

The Act states that on public holidays "all Government offices shall be closed", although the Prime Minister may direct that specific offices stay open. If you need anything from a government counter, such as a document or a permit, plan for it on a working day.

Heritage Malta museums and sites

Heritage Malta, which runs the national museums and archaeological sites, lists five closure days in its current leaflet: 1 January, Good Friday, and 24, 25 and 31 December. That covers places such as the National Museum of Archaeology, Fort St Elmo and the National War Museum, Hagar Qim and Mnajdra, the Ggantija Temples on Gozo and the Hal Saflieni Hypogeum. The other public holidays are not on that closure list, but hours can differ from a normal day, so check the Heritage Malta site before you go. As of November 2026, Heritage Malta also lists a Hypogeum closure from 18 to 24 January 2027. Check availability before planning your visit.

Shops, banks and businesses

Ask individual shops and banks for their holiday opening arrangements. If staying in Sliema, St Julian's or St Paul's Bay, check meal and shopping options in advance rather than relying on normal hours.

What keeps running

Buses run on public holidays, with holiday changes. Its December 2025 notice announced lunchtime suspensions and an early finish on Christmas Day and New Year's Day; check the new notice for your travel dates. Check Malta Public Transport's service alerts the week before you travel; our transport overview and the getting around Malta guide explain the network.

The Gozo Channel ferry between Cirkewwa and Mgarr operates on public holidays. In recent years it has paused crossings for a few hours around lunchtime on Christmas Day and New Year's Day so that crews can eat with their families, with departures and resumption times specified in each notice. The Gozo ferry guide covers the routes; confirm holiday times on the operator's site in December.

For flights at Malta International Airport, check your airline's schedule and allow extra time for the journey on holiday weekends.

The holidays worth planning a trip around

Carnival and St Paul's Shipwreck (February)

Festivals Malta lists Malta Carnival on 5 to 9 February 2027, before the Feast of St Paul's Shipwreck on 10 February. The feast commemorates the shipwreck of the apostle Paul on Malta, and the main celebration is in the capital. See our Valletta guide for the city itself.

L-Imnarja (29 June)

The Feast of St Peter and St Paul is better known by its Maltese name, L-Imnarja. Check the programme for celebrations at Buskett Gardens and on Gozo before choosing travel dates.

Santa Marija (15 August)

The Feast of Santa Marija falls on 15 August; check parish programmes for the celebrations. Plan transport and accommodation in advance for mid-August, including visits to beaches such as Mellieha Bay and Golden Bay, so book transport and rooms early if your trip covers it.

Victory Day (8 September)

The Victory Day Regatta in the Grand Harbour is the traditional event of the day, with rowing races watched from the waterfronts of Valletta and the Three Cities. The date is also the Feast of Our Lady of Victories. For the history behind the harbour's sieges, Fort St Angelo and Fort St Elmo are the places to go.

Freedom Day, Independence Day and Republic Day

The three political national holidays mark the steps to modern Malta: independence in 1964, the republic in 1974 and the closure of the last foreign military bases in 1979, which Freedom Day on 31 March commemorates. For visitors they are mostly normal days out with a public holiday mood.

Christmas and the Immaculate Conception

December has three holidays in 2027: 8 December, Republic Day on 13 December and Christmas Day. Our Malta in winter guide covers the Christmas season, cribs and what stays open.

Planning tips

  • Plan holiday weekends. In 2027, New Year's Day, St Joseph and Good Friday all fall on a Friday, and Sette Giugno and Republic Day on a Monday. Check ferry notices and accommodation availability on Gozo for those weekends.
  • Check Heritage Malta closures first. If a museum day is central to your plan, avoid 1 January, Good Friday and 24, 25 and 31 December.
  • Use the holidays for festivals. L-Imnarja, Santa Marija and Victory Day are among the best days of the year to see Maltese traditions up close. See the full events calendar and our best time to visit Malta guide.
  • Remember Sundays. Sunday is a public holiday by law, check business opening arrangements rather than assuming normal weekday hours.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many public holidays does Malta have in 2027?

Malta has 14 public holidays in 2027: five national holidays (Freedom Day, Sette Giugno, Victory Day, Independence Day and Republic Day) and nine other public holidays listed in the Schedule to the National Holidays and Other Public Holidays Act. Sundays are also public holidays by law.

When is Good Friday in Malta in 2027?

Good Friday falls on Friday 26 March 2027. Easter Sunday is 28 March. Easter Monday is not a public holiday in Malta.

Are public holidays moved to Monday in Malta if they fall on a weekend?

No. The holiday stays on its date. Since 1 January 2021, the law gives employees an extra day of vacation leave when a national or public holiday falls on a Saturday or Sunday, but no substitute weekday holiday is declared. In 2027 this applies to Workers' Day (Saturday 1 May), the Assumption (Sunday 15 August) and Christmas Day (Saturday 25 December).

Is Boxing Day a public holiday in Malta?

Boxing Day is not a separately named public holiday in Malta. However, 26 December 2027 is a Sunday, and Sundays are public holidays under the Act.

Are museums open on public holidays in Malta?

Heritage Malta closes its museums and sites on 1 January, Good Friday, and 24, 25 and 31 December. On the other public holidays they are not on the closure list, but check opening hours before you go, since sites can run shorter hours or close temporarily for restoration.

Do buses and the Gozo ferry run on public holidays?

Yes. Buses may have holiday timetables and service breaks; check the notice for your travel dates, and the Gozo Channel ferry operates between Cirkewwa and Mgarr. On Christmas Day and New Year's Day the ferry has paused for a few hours around lunchtime in recent years, so check the holiday schedule before travelling.

Which Malta public holidays are best for festivals?

L-Imnarja on 29 June at Buskett, the Feast of Santa Marija on 15 August and Victory Day on 8 September, with its regatta in the Grand Harbour, are the most festive. Good Friday brings Holy Week processions in many towns, and Festivals Malta lists Carnival 2027 on 5 to 9 February.

guides.title: Things to Do in Malta: A Guide by Interest
guides.summary: Things to do in Malta by interest: UNESCO temples and the Hypogeum, Valletta and the Three Cities, beaches and dives, Gozo, food, walks, kids and rainy days.
guides.html:
Malta is small enough that almost nothing is far away, yet it holds more than most visitors can fit into one trip. The Republic of Malta is three inhabited islands: Malta itself, Gozo to the northwest and tiny Comino between them. UNESCO lists three World Heritage properties here, the City of Valletta, the Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum and the Megalithic Temples of Malta, and the sea around the islands is clear enough to make diving and snorkelling a main reason to come. This guide groups the best things to do by interest, so you can build days around what you actually enjoy. Every item links to its own page with practical details.

History and the prehistoric temples

Malta's prehistoric monuments are the islands' most unusual draw. The Megalithic Temples of Malta were inscribed on the UNESCO list in 1980 and extended in 1992, and several of the component sites can be visited in a day or two.

  • Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum in Paola is an underground burial complex cut into limestone on three levels. Heritage Malta says it was in use between 4000 BC and 1500 BC. Only a small group enters at a time, so tickets sell out well ahead: book as soon as your dates are fixed. Children under six are not admitted. As of November 2026, Heritage Malta also lists a closure from 18 to 24 January 2027.
  • Tarxien Temples are a few minutes from the Hypogeum and pair well with it on the same morning.
  • Ħaġar Qim and Mnajdra sit on the southern cliffs above the sea, linked by a short path. Combine them with the boat trip into the Blue Grotto just along the coast.
  • Ġgantija Temples on Gozo are the reason many history fans cross on the ferry.
  • The National Museum of Archaeology in Valletta holds many of the finds from these sites and is the best place to start if you want context before visiting them.

Later history is everywhere too. In Rabat, the St Paul's Catacombs and the Domus Romana cover the Roman and early Christian centuries, while the walled hilltop of Mdina next door is a medieval town where you can visit St Paul's Cathedral.

Valletta and the Grand Harbour

Valletta is a compact walled capital built by the Knights of St John, and the whole city is a World Heritage property. Allow at least a full day to explore on foot.

  • St John's Co-Cathedral is the headline interior: plain outside, gilded and painted inside.
  • The Grandmaster's Palace was the seat of the Knights' Grand Masters.
  • Upper Barrakka Gardens give the classic view across the Three Cities and the harbour.
  • Fort St Elmo and the National War Museum guard the tip of the peninsula, with a museum covering Malta's military history.

Across the water, Birgu (Vittoriosa) has Fort St Angelo and the Inquisitor's Palace. Marsamxetto Steamferry Services operates ferries from Valletta to the Three Cities and to Sliema, avoiding road traffic. To see all the creeks and fortifications from sea level, take one of the Grand Harbour cruises. Valletta also hosts several of the year's biggest events, including Notte Bianca, the Malta International Fireworks Festival and the start of the Rolex Middle Sea Race, while Birgu has its own candlelit Birgufest.

Sea, beaches and diving

Malta's coastline is mostly rock, so the sandy beaches are precious and busy in summer. The best ones are in the north and northwest of Malta island.

  • Golden Bay and its neighbour Għajn Tuffieħa Bay face west, which makes them the place for a sunset swim.
  • Mellieħa Bay is a long sandy bay, the easiest choice for families.
  • Paradise Bay and Armier Bay are at the northern tip, close to the Gozo ferry.
  • In the south, St Peter's Pool is a natural rock pool on the Delimara headland, where people swim from flat limestone ledges.

Underwater, Malta is a serious destination. Scuba diving covers wrecks, caves and reefs around all three islands, and snorkelling is another way to explore rocky coves when sea conditions are suitable. On the surface, try sea kayaking along the cliffs, stand-up paddleboarding in calmer bays, or a day out on the water through sailing and yacht charters. For a full comparison of swimming spots, see our guide to the best beaches in Malta.

Gozo and Comino

Gozo is greener, quieter and slower than Malta, and it deserves more than a rushed day trip if you can spare it. The Gozo Channel car ferry from Ċirkewwa to Mġarr takes about 25 minutes, and a fast ferry runs from Valletta.

  • The Cittadella crowns Victoria, the island's main town, with walls you can walk around for views across the whole island.
  • Dwejra Bay and the Inland Sea on the west coast are a striking stretch of cliffs and sea caves.
  • Ta' Pinu Basilica stands alone in open countryside near Għarb and is a major place of pilgrimage.
  • Ramla Bay is the red-sand beach on Gozo's north coast; Xlendi Bay and Mġarr ix-Xini are narrow inlets good for swimming and snorkelling.
  • Gozo's quiet back roads make cycling in Gozo a good way to link villages.

Comino is almost uninhabited. Its Blue Lagoon is a popular swimming spot and gets very crowded in summer. Since May 2025, visitors arriving by boat who wish to go ashore at the Blue Lagoon have needed a free online booking for one of three daily time slots, with numbers capped at any one time. Check the current rules before you go, then pick one of the Comino boat trips. Our Comino and Blue Lagoon guide and Gozo travel guide go into more detail.

Food and drink

Maltese food borrows from Sicily, North Africa and Britain and adds its own staples. Start with pastizzi, flaky pastries filled with ricotta or peas, sold from small shops and kiosks across the islands. For lunch, a ftira or hobż biż-żejt, bread rubbed with tomato and topped with tuna, capers and olives, is the classic choice. A traditional dish is stuffat tal-fenek, slow-cooked rabbit.

Other dishes worth ordering include lampuki pie made with dolphin fish in season, aljotta fish soup, timpana, and bigilla, a bean dip. On Gozo, look for ġbejniet, small sheep's cheeses. Finish with imqaret. In Marsaxlokk, Visit Malta describes the Sunday fish market as a window on a traditional industry, and the harbour is lined with fish restaurants. To go deeper, book one of the food tours and cooking classes or a wine tasting of local grape varieties.

Walks and the outdoors

Malta is best walked outside the hot months. Coastal walking and hiking routes follow the cliffs on all three islands. Good places to start:

  • Dingli Cliffs, the high southwestern edge of Malta, for a coastal walk.
  • Majjistral Nature and History Park, the coastal strip between Golden Bay and Anchor Bay.
  • Buskett Gardens, a wooded valley below Dingli and the setting for the Mnarja festival on 29 June.
  • Xrobb l-Għaġin Nature Park on the Delimara peninsula near Marsaxlokk.
  • The Red Tower on the ridge above Mellieħa, a short climb with views towards Gozo.

Birdwatchers should look at the Għadira Nature Reserve behind Mellieħa Bay and the Simar Nature Reserve at Xemxija, both linked to birdwatching trips. Climbers will find sea cliffs and crags covered on our rock climbing page.

With children

Malta is easy with children: distances are short and many sights are compact. Ideas that work for most ages:

  • Popeye Village, a film set turned family attraction, overlooking Anchor Bay near Mellieħa.
  • The Malta National Aquarium in Qawra, a good half day in any weather.
  • Beach days at Mellieħa Bay, Pretty Bay at Birżebbuġa and the Bugibba Perched Beach, checking sea conditions and access before swimming.
  • Forts with ramparts and cannon, especially Fort St Elmo in Valletta.
  • Film location tours for older children who know the films and series shot on the islands.

Note that the Hypogeum does not admit children under six, so plan that visit for when someone can stay outside with the youngest.

Rainy days

Rain is rare in summer but does come in the cooler months, usually in short bursts. Indoor options are plentiful:

  • Valletta's museums: the National Museum of Archaeology, the National War Museum at Fort St Elmo and the Grandmaster's Palace.
  • St John's Co-Cathedral, which can easily take a couple of hours with the audio guide.
  • The Mosta Rotunda, a vast domed church in the middle of Malta.
  • The Hypogeum, the catacombs in Rabat and the Inquisitor's Palace in Birgu.
  • The aquarium in Qawra.

For what the weather is really like month by month, see our Malta weather page and the guide to Malta in winter.

Putting it together

For a first trip, three days covers Valletta, the temples and one beach day; five to seven days lets you add Gozo and Comino without rushing. Our ready-made 3-day, 5-day and 7-day itineraries turn the ideas above into day plans, and the getting around Malta guide covers buses, ferries and driving. If you are timing a trip around festivals, browse the events calendar and our best time to visit Malta guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the one thing not to miss in Malta?

For most visitors it is Valletta: the walled capital is a UNESCO World Heritage property and holds St John's Co-Cathedral, the Upper Barrakka Gardens and Fort St Elmo within walking distance. If prehistory interests you, the Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum is the rarest experience on the islands, but tickets are limited and need booking well ahead.

Do I need to book the Hypogeum in advance?

Yes. Heritage Malta describes it as a highly popular attraction and strongly recommends booking early, because only a small group enters at a time. A limited number of last-minute tickets may go on sale the day before at a higher price. Children under six are not admitted.

Is Gozo worth visiting on a short trip?

Yes, even for a day. The Gozo Channel ferry from Ċirkewwa to Mġarr takes about 25 minutes, and in one day you can see the Cittadella in Victoria, the Ġgantija Temples and a beach such as Ramla Bay. If you have five days or more, staying a night or two on Gozo lets you see it at a slower pace.

Do I need to book to visit the Blue Lagoon on Comino?

Visitors arriving by boat who wish to go ashore at the Blue Lagoon have needed a free online booking since May 2025, choosing one of three daily time slots, and access without a valid booking may lead to a fine. Rules can change between seasons, so check the official booking site before you travel.

What can I do in Malta when it rains?

Head indoors to Valletta's museums, including the National Museum of Archaeology and the National War Museum at Fort St Elmo, or spend a couple of hours in St John's Co-Cathedral. The Mosta Rotunda, the catacombs in Rabat, the Inquisitor's Palace in Birgu and the national aquarium in Qawra are other good choices.

What is there for children to do in Malta?

Popeye Village near Mellieħa and the Malta National Aquarium in Qawra are the obvious family days out. Shallow sandy beaches such as Mellieħa Bay and Pretty Bay suit younger swimmers, and Valletta's forts are fun to explore. Allow for traffic when planning journeys between them.

Which Maltese food should I try first?

Start with pastizzi, the ricotta or pea pastries sold across the islands, and a ftira for lunch. For dinner, rabbit stew (stuffat tal-fenek) is a traditional choice. On Gozo, try the small local cheeses called ġbejniet.

guides.title: Where to Stay in Malta: Best Areas by Traveller Type
guides.summary: Where to stay in Malta, area by area: Valletta, Sliema, St Julian’s, Bugibba, Mellieha, Mdina, the south and Gozo, with who each suits and how each connects.
guides.html:
Malta is small, but where you sleep changes the trip more than you might expect. The main island is densely built, traffic is heavy at peak times, and a bus ride from the north coast to Valletta can take far longer than the distance suggests. Choose a base near what you want to do most, whether that is museums, beaches, nightlife or quiet countryside, and use buses and ferries for the rest. This guide compares the main areas of Malta and Gozo, who each suits, the trade-offs, and how each connects to the airport and the rest of the islands. It names areas, not hotels.

Quick picks by traveller type

  • First visit, history and food: Valletta or the Three Cities.
  • Couples who want a seafront walk and easy transport: Sliema.
  • Nightlife and late dinners: St Julian's.
  • Families on a budget: St Paul's Bay, Bugibba and Qawra.
  • Sandy beaches and day trips to Gozo: Mellieħa.
  • Quiet, inland and central: Mdina and Rabat.
  • Slow pace, walking and countryside: Gozo.

Getting in: one airport, two ferry routes

Visitors arriving by air use Malta International Airport (MLA) at Luqa, in the south of the main island. Malta Public Transport's Airport Direct buses are one transfer option; regular airport bus routes can cost less. As of November 2026 they run as follows: TD1 to Rabat, Buġibba, Mellieħa and Ċirkewwa (hourly); TD2 to St Julian's and Pembroke and TD3 to St Julian's, Sliema, Gżira and Msida (both every 30 minutes); TD4 to Valletta and the Gozo fast ferry (every 30 minutes); and TD5 to Rabat and Buġibba (hourly). The fare is €3, or €3.50 on TD1.

For Gozo you have two choices. The Gozo Channel car ferry crosses from Ċirkewwa at the northern tip of Malta to Mġarr in about 25 minutes. Gozo Highspeed catamarans run from Valletta, and also from Sliema and Buġibba, for foot passengers. Your base decides which is easier, and our Gozo ferry guide has the details.

Valletta

The capital is the best base for a first visit if sightseeing comes first. Inside the walls you can walk to St John's Co-Cathedral, the Upper Barrakka Gardens, Fort St Elmo and the National Museum of Archaeology, and the main bus terminus is just outside the city gate. Ferries cross to Sliema and to the Three Cities, and the Gozo fast ferry leaves from the harbour below the city.

Suits: first-timers, couples, culture lovers, travellers without a car. Trade-offs: no sandy beach (you swim from rocks or travel to one), steep streets and many steps, and room size and lift access vary between properties. It can feel quiet late at night outside festival weekends such as Notte Bianca. Driving and parking in the city are best avoided.

The Three Cities across the Grand Harbour (Birgu, Senglea and Cospicua) offer a similar historic setting with fewer visitors. Birgu has Fort St Angelo and the Inquisitor's Palace, and the ferry to Valletta makes the capital an easy hop. Choose them if you want character and calm and do not mind fewer restaurants.

Sliema

Sliema faces Valletta across Marsamxett Harbour and is the most practical all-round base on the island. A long seafront promenade runs towards St Julian's, with rocky swimming areas and lidos along the way, and the area has plenty of shops, cafes and restaurants. The ferry to Valletta takes you to the capital without traffic, Airport Direct TD3 runs from the airport, and Gozo Highspeed also sails from Sliema. Many harbour cruises and Comino boat trips leave from the Sliema waterfront.

Suits: couples, first-timers who want more evening choice than Valletta, travellers relying on public transport. Trade-offs: heavy construction and traffic in places, few sandy beaches nearby, and many modern blocks rather than historic streets.

St Julian's

St Julian's runs on from Sliema around Spinola Bay and St George's Bay, one of the few sandy beaches in this part of the island. Its character changes block by block: Spinola Bay has waterfront restaurants, while Paceville is the nightlife quarter, with clubs and bars open late. Airport Direct TD2 and TD3 both serve the area.

Suits: nightlife, groups of friends, travellers who want lots of restaurants on the doorstep. Trade-offs: noise late at night if you stay close to Paceville, and crowds in summer. The UK government's travel advice warns of drink spiking in some Paceville bars, so buy your own drinks, keep them in sight and check your bill. Families and light sleepers should look at the quieter edges or at Sliema.

St Paul's Bay, Bugibba and Qawra

This is the main resort area in the north of Malta, with a long seafront promenade, a wide spread of apartments and mid-range hotels, and prices that are often lower than in Sliema and St Julian's. The Bugibba Perched Beach gives a small sandy area on the seafront, the Malta National Aquarium is in Qawra, and the Simar Nature Reserve is on the edge of town at Xemxija. Airport Direct TD1 and TD5 reach Buġibba, and Gozo Highspeed sails from Buġibba too.

Suits: families, budget travellers, longer stays, divers heading for northern sites. Trade-offs: busy and built-up, with fewer historic streets, and a long ride to Valletta and the south. It is a resort rather than a town with a historic core.

Mellieħa

Mellieħa sits on a ridge above Mellieħa Bay, a long sandy bay. It is the best-placed base for the northern beaches, including Paradise Bay, Armier Bay and Golden Bay, and for the Gozo Channel ferry at Ċirkewwa. Popeye Village, the Red Tower and the Għadira Nature Reserve are close by, and the Majjistral park coast is good walking country. TD1 links it to the airport.

Suits: beach-focused families and couples, anyone planning several days on Gozo and Comino, walkers. Trade-offs: far from Valletta and the southern temples, fewer evening options, and the village is on a hill above the beach. A car or a willingness to use buses helps.

Mdina and Rabat

The walled hilltop town of Mdina and the larger town of Rabat beside it sit in the middle of the island. Stay here for quiet evenings in historic streets and easy access to St Paul's Cathedral, the St Paul's Catacombs, the Domus Romana, Dingli Cliffs and Buskett Gardens. TD1 and TD5 run from the airport to Rabat.

Suits: couples, history lovers, walkers, return visitors who want something calmer. Trade-offs: limited accommodation and restaurants, no sea on the doorstep, and you will need buses or a car to reach beaches.

Marsaxlokk and the south

Marsaxlokk is Malta's main fishing harbour, full of painted luzzu boats, with fish restaurants on the waterfront and a Sunday fish market. Nearby you can swim at St Peter's Pool and Pretty Bay, walk in Xrobb l-Għaġin Nature Park, and reach the Hypogeum, the Tarxien Temples, Ħaġar Qim and Mnajdra and the Blue Grotto without crossing the whole island. The airport is in the south of the main island.

Suits: travellers who want a village atmosphere, food lovers, anyone focused on the prehistoric sites. Trade-offs: a small choice of places to stay, quiet evenings, a long trip to the north and to the Gozo ferry, and Sunday crowds at the market.

Gozo

Staying on Gozo changes the pace of a trip. Victoria, the island's main town, is central and close to the Cittadella; Xlendi in the southwest has a small seafront on Xlendi Bay; and Mġarr, the ferry port, is handy for early or late crossings. Many visitors rent farmhouses with pools in the villages. From any of them you can reach the Ġgantija Temples, Ramla Bay, Dwejra and Ta' Pinu Basilica, and Gozo makes a good base for diving, cycling and coastal walks. Comino is a short boat ride away.

Suits: walkers, divers, couples, families who want space, second or longer visits. Trade-offs: every trip to Valletta or the airport includes the ferry, and a car makes life easier, though buses cover the main villages from Victoria. Arriving late in the evening needs planning. See our Gozo travel guide.

Practical points before you book

  • Environmental contribution: as of November 2026, the Malta Tourism Authority lists a charge of €1.50 per person aged 18 or over per night in licensed accommodation, in force since 1 July 2026 and capped at €22.50 per person per visit. It is collected by the accommodation, and rates can change with national budget measures.
  • Split stays: on a week or longer, two bases work well, for example Valletta or Sliema for sightseeing and then Mellieħa or Gozo for beaches and walks.
  • Summer heat: check that your room has air conditioning from June to September, and that older townhouses in Valletta and Mdina are not up several flights of stairs if that matters to you.
  • Car or no car: in Valletta, Sliema and St Julian's a car is more trouble than help. On Gozo, in Mellieħa and in the south it saves time. Read getting around Malta before deciding.

For a wider introduction, read our Malta first-timers guide and things to do in Malta, or follow the 7-day itinerary, which pairs two bases.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is the best place to stay in Malta for a first visit?

Valletta or Sliema. Valletta puts the main sights, museums and the bus terminus within walking distance, while Sliema has more restaurants and a seafront promenade and is linked to Valletta by ferry. Both have direct Airport Direct buses: TD4 to Valletta and TD3 to Sliema.

Which area of Malta is best for families?

St Paul's Bay, Bugibba and Qawra, or Mellieħa. Bugibba and Qawra have a seafront promenade, a perched sandy beach, the national aquarium and generally lower prices. Mellieħa is next to the long sandy beach at Mellieħa Bay and close to Popeye Village.

Where should I stay in Malta for nightlife?

St Julian's, especially around Paceville, where bars and clubs stay open late. Light sleepers should pick the quieter edges of St Julian's or stay in Sliema. The UK government advises visitors to watch their drinks and check bills in some Paceville bars.

Should I stay on Gozo or Malta?

On a short first trip, base yourself on Malta and visit Gozo as a day trip: the Gozo Channel ferry from Ċirkewwa to Mġarr takes about 25 minutes. With a week or more, or if you prefer quiet countryside, walking and diving, spending some nights on Gozo is worthwhile.

Is Valletta a good base without a car?

Yes. Valletta is the hub of the bus network, ferries cross to Sliema and the Three Cities, the Gozo fast ferry leaves from its harbour, and, as of November 2026, Airport Direct TD4 runs every 30 minutes from the airport. Driving and parking in the city are difficult, so most visitors do without a car.

How much is the Malta tourist eco tax?

As of November 2026, the Malta Tourism Authority lists the environmental contribution at €1.50 per person per night for guests aged 18 and over, capped at €22.50 per person per visit, in force since 1 July 2026. It is collected by your accommodation.

Which part of Malta is closest to the airport?

Malta International Airport is at Luqa in the south of the main island. Valletta is served by Airport Direct TD4. Check the journey from your chosen accommodation, especially if staying in the north.

destinations.name: Comino
destinations.tagline: Car-free island between Malta and Gozo, home of the Blue Lagoon
destinations.summary: Comino is the tiny, car-free island between Malta and Gozo: the turquoise Blue Lagoon, quiet Santa Marija Bay and coastal walks, reached only by boat.
destinations.html:
Comino (Kemmuna) is the small island in the channel between Malta and Gozo. It has no towns and no cars, just rocky garrigue, a few tracks and a coastline of coves and caves. Comino is part of the protected Natura 2000 network. For most visitors Comino means one place: the Blue Lagoon, a shallow channel of clear turquoise water between Comino and the islet of Cominotto.

The Blue Lagoon gets very crowded on summer days, when boats arrive from Malta and Gozo through the morning. To protect the site, the Malta Tourism Authority introduced a free online booking system in May 2025, with a cap of 4,000 visitors at any one time and three daily time slots. As of November 2026, the MTA says visitors arriving by private or commercial vessel must pre-book before setting foot at the Blue Lagoon. Obtain your QR code before travelling and follow the booked time slot. Bring shade, water and sun protection, as there are only basic kiosks.

What to do

  • Swim and snorkel in the Blue Lagoon in the early morning, before most boats arrive.
  • Walk to the quieter sandy cove of Santa Marija Bay on the north side.
  • Follow the tracks up to St Mary's Tower, a Knights-era watchtower on the south cliffs.
  • See the sea caves on a boat trip or by sea kayak.

The water around Comino is also a favourite for diving, with caves and reefs off the western cliffs. In spring the island is green and good for walking, and the paths are almost empty compared with the lagoon in August.

Comino is reached only by boat. Short shuttle crossings leave from Cirkewwa and Marfa in the north of Malta and from Mgarr in Gozo, and longer day cruises depart from Sliema and Bugibba. Nearly everyone visits as a day trip from Mellieha, the north coast or Gozo. Our Comino and Blue Lagoon guide has more planning detail.

destinations.name: Gozo
destinations.tagline: Greener sister island of temples, citadel and quiet bays
destinations.summary: Gozo is Malta's slower, greener sister island: the Ggantija temples, the Cittadella in Victoria, red-sand Ramla Bay and dive sites, a 25-minute ferry from Malta.
destinations.html:
Gozo (Ghawdex) lies northwest of Malta across a narrow channel, with Comino in between. It is smaller, greener and more rural than the main island, a landscape of flat-topped hills, terraced fields and farming villages, each with a large parish church. The pace is noticeably slower, which is the reason many visitors come, either on a day trip or for a few nights away from Malta's busier towns.

The capital, Victoria, also called Rabat, sits in the middle of the island under the walls of the Cittadella, the fortified old town with a cathedral and views over the whole island. On the Xaghra plateau, the Ggantija Temples date from the Late Neolithic and are part of the Megalithic Temples of Malta World Heritage Site. On the west coast, Dwejra has the Inland Sea and dramatic cliffs, and the Ta' Pinu Basilica stands alone in the fields near Gharb.

What to do

  • Walk the bastions of the Cittadella and visit the Ggantija Temples on the same day.
  • Swim at Ramla Bay, San Blas, Xlendi, Hondoq ir-Rummien or Mgarr ix-Xini.
  • Dive the Gozo coast; scuba diving is one of the island's main draws.
  • Explore the lanes and hills on a cycling trip, then try gbejniet cheeselets.

Marsalforn and Xlendi are Gozo's two main resorts, both small bays with restaurants and hotels. Many visitors stay in converted farmhouses with pools in the villages. The Feast of Santa Marija on 15 August is a major celebration in Victoria.

Gozo Channel's ferry from Cirkewwa, at Malta's northern tip, to Mgarr takes about 25 minutes, and foot passengers' tickets are checked in Gozo on the return trip. A fast passenger ferry also runs from Valletta's Grand Harbour to Mgarr. Buses cover the island from Victoria, but a car or a tour helps on a day trip. See the Gozo ferry guide and the Gozo travel guide for details.

destinations.name: Marsaxlokk
destinations.tagline: Southern fishing harbour of painted luzzu boats and a Sunday market
destinations.summary: Marsaxlokk is Malta's main fishing harbour: painted luzzu boats, a Sunday fish market and seafood lunches, with St Peter's Pool and the south's temples nearby.
destinations.html:
Marsaxlokk sits on a wide bay on the southeast coast, a few kilometres from the airport. Visit Malta calls it the islands' main fishing harbour, and the bay is full of luzzus, the traditional Maltese fishing boats painted in bright blue, yellow, red and green, with an eye painted on the prow. The village is small and low-rise, and life still revolves around the boats, the nets and the fish.

The Sunday fish market along the waterfront is the reason most visitors come. Stalls sell the night's catch beside general market stalls of honey, lace, sweets and souvenirs, and the busiest hours are in the morning. On other days the harbour is calmer, and the waterfront restaurants serve grilled fish and local dishes such as aljotta fish soup and, in autumn, lampuki pie.

What to do

  • Arrive early on Sunday for the fish market, then stay for a long seafood lunch.
  • Swim from the flat rocks at St Peter's Pool on the Delimara peninsula.
  • Walk the coastal trails of the Xrobb l-Ghagin Nature Park above the open sea.
  • Combine the village with Pretty Bay in nearby Birzebbuga.

The south coast's prehistoric and natural highlights are within a short drive. Hagar Qim and Mnajdra stand on the cliffs above the sea, and the boats into the Blue Grotto leave from Wied iz-Zurrieq nearby. Closer to the harbour, the Tarxien Temples and the Hypogeum make a full southern day.

Marsaxlokk is reached by road from the airport, with direct buses from Valletta. There are few hotels, so most people visit for a morning or an afternoon from Valletta, the Three Cities or Sliema. Parking is tight on Sundays; the bus is often the easier choice.

destinations.name: Mdina and Rabat
destinations.tagline: The walled former capital and the catacomb town outside its gates
destinations.summary: Mdina is Malta's walled hilltop former capital, quiet and lamplit at night. Rabat, just outside its walls, adds St Paul's Catacombs, the Domus Romana and village life.
destinations.html:
Mdina crowns a ridge in the centre of Malta, and its bastions look out over most of the island. Through the Middle Ages and until the Order of St John arrived in 1530, it was the island's capital. The Knights moved their base to the harbour and then to Valletta, and Mdina became the quiet home of the old noble families. Visit Malta calls it the silent city and one of Europe's finest examples of an ancient walled city. Few cars are allowed inside, and at night its lanes are lit by lamps.

Inside the walls, St Paul's Cathedral dominates the main square, and Bastion Square gives a wide view across the island toward the coast. Rabat (Ir-Rabat) begins right outside the gate and is a living town with shops, bakeries and churches. Here you find the Domus Romana, a Roman townhouse with fine mosaic floors found by chance in 1881, the underground passages of St Paul's Catacombs, and St Paul's Grotto beneath the parish church, linked by tradition to the apostle's stay in Malta.

What to do

  • Walk Mdina's lanes early in the morning or after the tour groups leave.
  • Go underground at St Paul's Catacombs, part of a cemetery whose history goes back to at least the 3rd or 4th century BC.
  • See the mosaics of the Domus Romana on the edge of Rabat.
  • Drive or cycle on to Dingli Cliffs and the woodland of Buskett Gardens.

Buskett hosts Mnarja on 29 June, one of Malta's oldest traditional feasts, with folk singing and rabbit stew. Mdina's walls also appear on several film location tours.

The pair sit roughly in the middle of the island, reached by road from the airport, with buses from Valletta and the resort towns. Most visitors come for a day, but a night in a Mdina or Rabat guesthouse lets you see the old city after dark, when it is at its quietest. The Mosta Rotunda is a short drive northeast.
